articles.title: Air quality worsens in Metro Cebu amid haze from Indonesia
articles.summary: CEBU CITY — Air quality in Metro Cebu deteriorated further on Wednesday as transboundary haze from ongoing forest fires in Indonesia continued to affect the region. The Environmental Management…

blocks.text: CEBU CITY — Air quality in Metro Cebu deteriorated further on Wednesday as transboundary haze from ongoing forest fires in Indonesia continued to affect the region.
The Environmental Management Bureau (EMB) of the Department of Environment and Natural Resources (DENR) in Central Visayas detected “acute unhealthy levels” of pollutants in Metro Cebu.
The air quality index (AQI) reached 203 on Wednesday, up from 173 on Tuesday.
In response, the bureau advised the public, particularly those with existing respiratory conditions, to stay indoors.
Others were urged to wear face masks, stay hydrated, and take other precautions to reduce their exposure to polluted air.
Despite the worsening air quality, the Department of Health in Central Visayas (DOH-7) said there had been no reported hospital admissions related to the haze as of Wednesday.

Still, rural health units (RHUs) have been advised to prepare for a possible increase in consultations involving health effects linked to the haze, said Dr. Van Philip Baton, chief of the Local Health Support Division of DOH-7.

“We’re anticipating a possible increase in asthma, so we may see this in our RHU and private clinics… So a reminder to the public is to consult immediately if they have any history of asthma or chronic obstructive pulmonary disease,” he said.
Baton also advised the public against self-medication, particularly those with asthma or other chronic respiratory conditions.
Arthur Niño Calupig, air quality monitoring specialist at EMB-7, said the transboundary movement of pollutants caused the deteriorating air quality.
Smoke from fires in Kalimantan, Indonesia, was being carried toward the Philippines by the habagat, or southwest monsoon.
Calupig said the haze could persist for several more days if the fires continue to burn and prevailing wind patterns remain unchanged./coa

articles.title: Escudero seeks for public patience amid Poa's testimony
articles.summary: Senate impeachment court presiding officer Francis “Chiz” Escudero on Wednesday asked for the understanding and patience of the public and senator-judges as the defense and prosecution panels clashed…

blocks.text: Published September 2, 2026 2:13pm

Senate impeachment court presiding officer Francis “Chiz” Escudero on Wednesday asked for the understanding and patience of the public and senator-judges as the defense and prosecution panels clashed amid the testimony of Atty. Michael Poa in the trial.

Escudero said this on the 21st day of the impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte, as prosecution counsel and spokesperson Benjamin Tolosa Jr. and defense lead counsel Sheila Sison exchanged heated words while Poa was on the witness stand to testify on the alleged misuse of confidential funds.

“Para sa kaalaman din po ng kapwa ko senator-judges at mga sumusubaybay, mahirap na nga po na may dalawang abogadong nagkakaroon ng tagisan ng talino, gawin pa nating tatlo. Kaya pag-unawa lang po at pasensya ang hinihiling namin,” the presiding officer said.

(For the information of my fellow senator-judges and those watching the proceedings, it is difficult enough for two lawyers to have a battle of wits, let alone three. So we just ask for understanding and patience.)
“Parte po ito ng proseso para mapangalagaan hindi lamang ang karapatan ng respondent, pero pati ng testigo,” he added.
(This is part of the process to protect not only the rights of the respondent, but also the rights of the witness.)
Poa, who is part of the defense team, was called by the House prosecution team as witness in the trial. On Wednesday, he was declared as a hostile witness by the impeachment court.
At one point during Poa’s direct examination, Escudero said that he could no longer understand the points that the counsels were raising as Tolosa and Sison were at each other's throats.
While Tolosa was offering the testimony of the witness, he alleged that the Vice President chose Poa as “the man who knew nothing” to answer the state auditors.
Sison countered, saying that Tolosa’s claims “sound really just rhetoric aimed to provide drama in this proceeding.”
Escudero later ruled to strike off the record the line “abogadong walang alam” (lawyer who knows nothing) from Tolosa’s offer of testimony following Sison’s objection.
Tolosa and Sison also argued regarding the presentation of playback videos of former House Committee on Good Government and Public Accountability hearings during the trial.
Poa served as undersecretary, chief of staff, and spokesperson of DepEd during Duterte’s stint as Education secretary. — RSJ, GMA News

articles.title: Agana Bridge to reopen soon; P300M for repair of Tarlac bridges – Marcos
articles.summary: MANILA, Philippines – The national government will allocate P300 million for the rehabilitation of two bridges that partially collapsed due to strong river currents and continuous heavy rains,…

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines – The national government will allocate P300 million for the rehabilitation of two bridges that partially collapsed due to strong river currents and continuous heavy rains, President Ferdinand R. Marcos Jr. said on Wednesday.
Marcos made the announcement after inspecting the Agana and Aquino bridges in Tarlac City.
In a statement, Marcos said the Agana bridge could reopen to pedestrians within one week and to light vehicles weighing 10 tons or less within two weeks.

“We will be giving P300 million to the local government dahil ito ay local bridge. Kaya sila kailangan ng magkatrabaho dito. Siyempre tutulungan natin, tutulungan sa technical aspects that will help them in everything, every way that we can,” Marcos said.

(We will be giving P300 million to the local government because this is a local bridge. They will be responsible for carrying out the necessary work here. Of course, we will assist them, particularly with the technical aspects, and help them in every way that we can.)

“And of course, local government and national government magtutulungan para maging mas mabilis. Like I say, I hope in two weeks, they assure me that in two weeks there will already be light traffic allowed across Agana Bridge,” he added.

(And of course, the local government and the national government will work together to expedite the repairs. As I said, I hope that within two weeks, they have assured me that light traffic will already be allowed to cross Agana Bridge.)
Marcos noted that the volume of water brought by the recent rains was unprecedented, contributing to the bridge’s collapse.
He said the government would continue to adjust to better protect infrastructure from the effects of climate change.

“This bridge has been standing since just after the war. So 70 years old na ito. Sa buong karanasan ng Pilipinas ngayon lang tayo nakatikim ng ganitong klaseng ulan, ganitong klaseng pagbaha dahil nagbabago ang panahon dahil sa climate change,” he said.

(This bridge has been standing since just after the war, so it is around 70 years old. In the entire experience of the Philippines, this is the first time we have experienced this kind of rainfall and flooding, as the climate continues to change due to climate change.)
The Agana Bridge partially collapsed at around 7:40 p.m. on August 29 due to strong and surging floodwaters from the Tarlac River.
It gave way just a day after the nearby Aquino Bridge also collapsed, forcing motorists to take the Agana Bridge as an alternative route.
While the Agana Bridge is expected to accommodate light traffic within two weeks, Marcos said the Aquino Bridge could take longer to reopen due to the extent of the damage. /gsg

articles.title: Sports, art programs pushed to unlock students’ pent-up energy
articles.summary: MANILA, Philippines—Sports, music, and arts programs must be strengthened for students to release their “unspent energy,” Department of Education governance and operations Undersecretary…

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines—Sports, music, and arts programs must be strengthened for students to release their “unspent energy,” Department of Education governance and operations Undersecretary Malcolm Garma said Wednesday, amid discussions on social media use.
Calls for tighter regulation of social media and gaming platforms resurfaced following the fatal school shootings in Tacloban City on June 22 and Zamboanga City on August 18.

“So ang belief ko po is there are so much unspent energy among our learners. Hindi po pinapawisan so they resort to other forms to release the energy,” Garma said during the Kapihan sa Manila Prince Hotel forum on Wednesday.
(“So my belief is there are so much unspent energy among our learners. They are not sweating so they resort to other forms to release the energy.”)
“Siguro dahil sa cellphone, bihira na yung batang nakaka-appreciate ng kapaligiran, tumitingala sa langit at tinitignan ang ganda ng mga bituin,” he said.
(“Perhaps because of mobile phones, few children nowadays appreciate their surroundings, look up at the sky, and gaze at the beauty of the stars,” he said.)
Garma particularly recommended boosting outdoor activities, such as scouting, aside from strengthening physical education and sports clubs.
He said they are partnering with the Philippine Sports Commission and the National Youth Commission to implement these extracurricular activities.
Garma said a total ban on social media is not necessary, as it can also serve as an educational tool.
He added technology could be used as a learning tool, particularly when students are unable to attend school due to class suspensions during disasters.
Earlier at the forum, the Philippine National Police–Anti-Cybercrime Group director Maj. Gen. Wilson Asueta called for establishing a regulatory body to oversee social media and gaming platforms.
Last week, the Senate committee on public information and mass media, chaired by Sen. Robinhood Padilla, endorsed for plenary approval a bill setting 16 as the minimum age for social media use.

Senate Bill No. 2424, or the proposed Child Online Safety and Protection Act, seeks to regulate minors’ access to social media and require platforms to strengthen safeguards against online threats. /gsg

articles.title: ‘Tagisan ng talino’: 3 lawyers face off at Sara Duterte’s impeachment trial
articles.summary: MANILA, Philippines — What happens when a defense lawyer becomes a witness for the prosecution team in the impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte? At the witness stand on the 21st day of…

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines — What happens when a defense lawyer becomes a witness for the prosecution team in the impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte?

At the witness stand on the 21st day of the trial on Wednesday is Duterte’s defense lawyer and spokesperson Michael Poa, with private prosecutor Benjamin “Jay” Tolosa Jr. conducting the direct examination of the witness, and lawyer Sheila Sison leading Duterte’s defense team.
The Senate impeachment court declared Poa a hostile witness after he was called to the stand by the prosecution team.

As Tolosa began his direct examination of Poa, presiding officer Francis Escudero noted the growing tension between two opposing counsels, prompting him to call for understanding and patience from fellow senator-judges and the public.

blocks.caption: House prosecution counsel Benjamin “Jay” Tolosa Jr.

blocks.text: “Mahirap na nga po na may dalawang abogadong nagkakaroon ng tagisan ng talino, gawin pa nating tatlo.” Escudero said. “Kaya pang-unawa lang po at pasensya ang hinihihling namin. Parte po ito ng proseso para mapangalagaan, hindi lamang ang karapatan ng respondent, pero pati ng testigo.”

(It is already difficult when two lawyers are engaged in a battle of wits, and now we are making it three,” Escudero said. “So we are only asking for your understanding and patience. This is part of the process to safeguard not only the rights of the respondent but also those of the witness.)

The tension between Tolosa and Sison became more apparent when the private prosecutor questioned Poa about the P112.5 million in confidential funds released to DepEd when Duterte was secretary from 2022 to 2024.
Poa was Duterte’s chief of staff and spokesperson when she was at the DepEd.

Citing a 2015 joint circular of the Commission on Audit, Tolosa pointed out a provision that requires documentary evidence to prove the success of information given by informants in exchange of a cash reward.

“Sa madaling salita, dapat yun hong binigay na information na binayaran using a reward, dapat dahil dito sa informtion na ito nagkaroon ng success of information gathering and/or survellance activities…” the private prosecutor asked.
(In other words, the information for which a reward was paid should have resulted in the successful gathering of information and/or the conduct of surveillance activities.)
“Generally, and I say generally because hindi ko po alam…” Poa answered but he was cut by Tolosa.
Sison asked that Poa be allowed to complete his answer, noting that he could not even finish his sentence because he was stopped by the prosecutor.
“No, no first of all, Your Honor, with all due respect, this is not just an ordinary witness. He is a very experienced and competent counsel,” Tolosa said.
“Second, (Poa) is not just any counsel, not just any lawyer. He himself is the counsel in this very same proceedings of the respondent,” he added.
He then asked the court to strictly implement the rules of court, which, he said, requires a witness to answer yes or no to leading questions.

blocks.caption: Defense chief counsel Shiela Sison (Photo from Senate PRIB)

blocks.text: But Sison disputed this, saying “there’s nothing in the rules that provide for the allowance of questions that can only be answerable by yes or no.”
“In fact, what the rules of courts state is that the answers of the witness must be responsive. And so the witness is not the prohibited from giving responsive answers, Your Honor,” she pointed out.

“I’m not dictating the prosecutor what to ask. I’m merely asking that he does not interrupt the witness because, according to him, the witness is intelligent, the witness is smart. He can answer for himself,” Sison explained.
“The problem earlier was that he cut the witness off in the process of answering when he doesn’t even know yet what the answer of the witness is,” she added.
But Tolosa noted Sison’s own statement “that the witness can only give responsive responnses to questions.”
“Hence, if the answer that you’re eliciting, the question is clearly answerable by yes or no, any answer that does not conform to that is not responsive,” he told the senator-judges.
“Hence, we may ask that it be stricken off the record if it’s given or we may prevent the witness from giving it in the first place,” he said.
Escudero later ruled that there was nothing in the rules that would limit or constrict a witness to a mere yes or no answer, “and it should be responsive as correctly pointed out by Atty. Tolosa.”
“That’s the risk you run with a hostile and intelligent witness, Atty. Jay,” the presiding officer said, directing his statement to Tolosa.
(Note: The English translations in the article were AI-generated. )

articles.title: Bonoan clinically stable; discharge up to Sandiganbayan – PNP hospital
articles.summary: MANILA, Philippines—Former Public Works and Highways secretary Manuel Bonoan is clinically stable but under maintenance medication, according to Lt. Col Benaly Bayani, chief for internal medicine of…

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines—Former Public Works and Highways secretary Manuel Bonoan is clinically stable but under maintenance medication, according to Lt. Col Benaly Bayani, chief for internal medicine of the Philippine National Police (PNP) General Hospital.

“Si Engineer Bonoan presently clinically stable po siya, controlled sa ngayon ang hypertension niya, under medication sa supervision ng ating medical team,” Bayani told reporters at Camp Crame on Wednesday.
(“Engineer Bonoan is currently clinically stable; his hypertension is under control, and he is on medication under the supervision of our medical team.”)
Bonoan was accused of involvement in an alleged P573-million kickback scheme linked to the infrastructure corruption scandal, and remains at the PNP General Hospital.
On Tuesday, the Sandiganbayan Fifth Division dropped Bonoan as an accused in the plunder and graft charges he was facing.
Asked when Bonoan could be discharged from hospital arrest, Bayani said in Filipino, “It depends on them (Sandiganbayan) what order they will give us.”
“Kung maalala ninyo dati na siya may medical condition so kinontinue lang namin kung ano ang medical treatment and regarding doon sa update yun lang naman ang instruction sa akin,” said Bayani.
(“If you recall, he already had a medical condition before, so we simply continued with his existing medical treatment. As for the update, that’s the only instruction I was given.”)

A medical certificate dated May 29, issued by Bonoan’s personal physician, showed that he was diagnosed with Stage IV chronic renal disease, hypertension, diabetes mellitus, gouty arthritis, spondylolisthesis, a spinal condition, and prostate cancer.
Bayani said Bonoan’s blood pressure is under control and he continues to attend hearings without any medical issues.
She also said that Bonoan is no longer using a wheelchair and can walk. / gsg

articles.title: Iloilo mayor urges caution amid haze from Indonesia
articles.summary: ILOILO CITY – Iloilo City Mayor Raisa Treñas has warned the public about the health risks of the very fine particles carried by the wind as a haze continues to blanket this city and Western Visayas.…

blocks.text: ILOILO CITY – Iloilo City Mayor Raisa Treñas has warned the public about the health risks of the very fine particles carried by the wind as a haze continues to blanket this city and Western Visayas.
“This could cause coughing, throat irritation, chest discomfort, and eye watering, and is dangerous for those with asthma and cardiovascular diseases,” Treñas said.
She strongly advised all residents, especially the elderly, pregnant women, and individuals with pre-existing conditions, to wear face masks, preferably N95, to prevent potential harm from the haze.

The Office of Civil Defense Region 6 has also released a comprehensive haze advisory, outlining critical precautionary measures for the public, especially limiting outdoor activities to minimize prolonged exposure. It warned that haze can irritate the eyes, nose, and throat, and worsen existing respiratory and cardiovascular issues.
The agency also advised wearing masks when venturing outdoors and securing homes against haze by using damp cloths to seal gaps where the dangerous particulates might enter.

A blanket of transboundary haze has descended upon this city and parts of Western Visayas, prompting local officials to issue health warnings and urge residents, particularly vulnerable groups, to take immediate precautions.
The haze, driven by persistent forest fires in Kalimantan, Indonesia, is carried northward across Philippine airspace by the prevailing southwest monsoon (habagat).
The Iloilo City Operations Center issued an advisory at 5:00 p.m. on Tuesday, confirming that the particulate matter is being channeled at an altitude of some three kilometers.

While a moderate haze layer was present in the morning, officials warned that lighter surface winds in the afternoon could reduce dispersion. This will trap fine particulate matter closer to the ground and worsen air quality.

The Environmental Management Bureau (EMB) Region VI station at the Garden of Love recorded a transition in the PM2.5 Air Quality Index (AQI) from “Good” late last week to “Fair” (AQI 70) by August 31. More concerning, real-time measurements from the Central Philippine University / Ungka Station registered a US AQI of 116, categorized as “Unhealthy for Sensitive Groups.” /coa

articles.title: Zaldy Co’s co-accused asks for house arrest amid stroke
articles.summary: MANILA, Philippines — The co-accused of former Ako Bicol party-list Rep. Zaldy Co asked a Sandiganbayan division if she could be placed under house arrest after suffering from a stroke. Juliet Calvo,…

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines — The co-accused of former Ako Bicol party-list Rep. Zaldy Co asked a Sandiganbayan division if she could be placed under house arrest after suffering from a stroke.

Juliet Calvo, the former maintenance division chief of the Department of Public Works and Highways (DPWH) in Region IV-B, faces a malversation case filed against her and eight other co-accused under the jurisdiction of the anti-graft court.
The Sandiganbayan Sixth Division on Wednesday conducted a hearing for Calvo’s pending hospital and house arrest motions.
“The motions of accused Calvo are submitted for resolution,” said Associate Justice Lord Villanueva after the hearing.
Calvo suffered from a stroke on Aug. 5 which led to a total paralysis, her lawyer Edwin Labro told the court on Aug. 13.

During the Aug. 13 hearing, Labro only filed an urgent motion for hospital arrest, but he told reporters he lodged another motion for Calvo’s house arrest “last week” amid developments on her medical condition.
Labro presented Dr. Anthony Lontoc, who testified before the court via teleconferencing.
“I would at least recommend hospital arrest or house arrest as long as the environment is well-suited for her situation,” Lontoc told the court.

Lontoc, who was Calvo’s physician since 2018, said her condition has improved, noting that the accused is only “50 percent paralyzed on her left” unlike “for the first two weeks” when she was “completely paralyzed.”
“As of now while there is still improvement, she still needs someone to take care of her,” the doctor said.
Calvo is still confined in a private hospital, and prosecutors did not object to her continuous confinement.
In July 21, Calvo took the witness stand to defend herself, saying her signing of a document which led to the release of funds for an allegedly anomalous project is just ministerial.
The Supreme Court said an act is only considered ministerial when it does not require the exercise of discretion or judgement and was just in obedience to the mandate of a legal authority.
Calvo’s case stemmed from a P289.4 million worth of road dike project in Naujan, Oriental Mindoro built by Sunwest which DPWH found to have serious structural deficiencies.

Sunwest is co-founded by Co, who could not participate in the trial as he was at large abroad, which prompted the court to declare him as a fugitive from justice, barring him from participating in the proceedings unless he surrendered voluntarily. /jpv

articles.title: Marcos says decades-old flood control plan finally being implemented
articles.summary: MANILA, Philippines – President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. on Wednesday said the flood control master plan, which had been left untouched for decades, is finally being implemented. He made the remarks…

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines – President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. on Wednesday said the flood control master plan, which had been left untouched for decades, is finally being implemented.
He made the remarks after inspecting the Aquino and Agana bridges in Tarlac City, which partially collapsed due to strong river currents and continuous heavy rains brought by the southwest monsoon.
“We already have a master plan; it’s just never been executed,” Marcos responded when asked if the public can expect a flood control master plan.

“We’re only executing it now. We have had a master plan for decades, but walang ginawa (but nothing was done). Hanggang ngayon lang. Ngayon lang natin sinisimulan (We’re only starting it now. We’re only doing it now),” he continued, not specifying that masterplan he was referring to.
These remarks came as 9.4 million people, or 2.7 million families, across Luzon were displaced by flooding caused by three storms and the prevailing southwest monsoon, or habagat, since August 1.
The National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Council also reported 39 fatalities, 20 people injured, and three others missing.

In the same statement, Marcos said the national government will allocate P300 million for the rehabilitation of the Agana and Aquino bridges that partially collapsed from strong river currents and continuous heavy rains.

He said the Agana bridge could reopen to pedestrians within one week and to light vehicles weighing 10 tons or less within two weeks. The Aquino Bridge, meanwhile, could take longer to reopen due to the extent of the damage. /jpv

articles.title: Almost half of world’s farmers poisoned by pesticides every year, experts find
articles.summary:
Study reveals that pesticide poisoning kills 11,000 people each year, with India accounting for nearly 60% of fatalities

Almost half of the world’s farmers are poisoned by pesticides every…

blocks.text: Almost half of the world’s farmers are poisoned by pesticides every single year, a study has found.

Using publicly available data from 2006-2023, the study, which was commissioned by Pesticide Action Network, found there to be an estimated 402-433m cases of unintentional acute pesticide poisoning of farmers and farm workers every year.

Based on a worldwide farming population of 934 million, this means approximately 46% of farmers are being poisoned every year. The greatest estimated number of poisonings was in southern Asia, followed by south-east Asia and east Africa.
The overall highest national incidence of poisoning was in Burkina Faso in west Africa, where nearly 84% of farmers and farm workers were reported to have experienced poisoning.

blocks.caption: Young farm workers harvesting cotton in a field near Boromo in Burkina Faso. Photograph: Issouf Sanogo/AFP/Getty

blocks.text: The study, published in the journal Frontiers in Public Health on Wednesday, also found that an estimated 11,000 deaths occur every year due to pesticide poisoning, with nearly 60% of these in India.
Jayakumar Chelaton, the executive director of Pesticide Action Network India, said the research exposed a “crisis that can no longer be ignored”.
The authors of the study are calling for “immediate action”, including the implementation of a UN recommendation to phase out highly hazardous pesticides.
The study states that despite global efforts to highlight the dangers, pesticide use has continued to grow steadily, with 3.8m tonnes used in 2023, a doubling since 1990.

Dr Sheila Willis, the head of international programmes at Pesticide Action Network UK, said: “Now that the scale of suffering has been revealed, farmers must be supported to access safer alternatives to protect their health and that of their families.”

The study did not consider the impact of pesticide exposure on the estimated 84 million children working in agriculture and did not look at the long-term health impacts, with acute pesticide poisoning defined in the study as any illness or health effect experienced a short time after exposure.
after newsletter promotion

Génon Jensen, the executive director of the Health and Environment Alliance, said: “We are extremely concerned about the devastating health impacts from pesticide poisonings – both the acute impacts mentioned in this study but also chronic exposures that farm workers and communities suffer.”

Hélène Nicora, the director general of Parkinson’s Europe, said there was also “overwhelming evidence” to suggest that Parkinson’s was an environmentally driven disease, with growing evidence linking pesticide exposure to the development of Parkinson’s.

Parkinson’s disease is a progressive disorder in which parts of the brain become damaged over time, affecting movement and balance. The global burden of the disease is rising, with France, Germany and Italy all recognising it as an occupational disease for farmers.
Farmers and farm workers are mainly exposed to pesticides during preparation and application, as well as when touching treated crops and contaminated equipment or clothing.

Speaking at a webinar organised by Friends of the Earth Europe earlier this year, Rendert Algra said he believed his Parkinson’s disease was linked to the pesticides he had used when working at his family farm in the Netherlands.
“Being the eldest son, I did all the spraying of pesticides in our fields for several years in a row,” he said.

Despite being the most robust study to date, the report highlights that available information on pesticide poisoning is inadequate, with the authors calling for standardised surveillance and reporting protocols so that pesticide-related poisonings become reliable and comparable.

articles.title: Ukrainian film-maker criticises EU after it cuts Venice Biennale funding over Russia controversy
articles.summary:
Sergei Loznitsa likens removal of €2m grant to ‘a punishment in kindergarten’ on eve of Venice film festival

One of Ukraine’s most acclaimed film-makers has criticised the European…

blocks.text: One of Ukraine’s most acclaimed film-makers has criticised the European Commission’s decision to cut off funds to the Venice Biennale over the opening of Russia’s pavilion, likening it to “a punishment in kindergarten”.
The Biennale drew heavy criticism this spring when it allowed Russia to use its pavilion for the first time since 2022, despite the ongoing full-scale invasion of Ukraine.

Speaking on the eve of the Biennale’s cinematic branch, the Venice film festival, the director Sergei Loznitsa said that while he would “never ever” personally visit the Russian pavilion, the row was a distraction from the EU’s own failure to enforce more effective economic sanctions against Moscow.

“The question I ask myself is this: can the existence of this Russian pavilion stop this war or not?” said Loznitsa, who won wide acclaim for his 2014 documentary Maidan and last year’s Soviet-set drama Two Prosecutors, and is showing his new film Imperium out of competition on the Lido this year.

blocks.caption: Loznitsa’s new documentary Imperium uses archival footage from the early 1970s filmed in the former Soviet Union. Photograph: Essential Filmproduktion, Kino Produzioni, Société Parisienne de Production, Studio Uljana Kim - footage courtesy of AAMOD

blocks.text: He added: “What I do know is that in the second quarter of this year, European companies imported gas from Russia at unprecedented levels, and all that money goes straight into bombs that fall on Ukraine.”

According to the EU’s Agency for the Cooperation of Energy Regulators, European imports of Russian liquified fossil gas increased by 17% compared with the same period in 2025, before a full EU-wide ban on Russian gas from 2027.
Loznitsa said: “This is a much more serious issue than whether there is a Russian pavilion in Venice or not. Cutting off funding to the Biennale is like a punishment in kindergarten.”

While the Russian pavilion’s exhibition The Tree is Rooted in the Sky was only accessible during the pre-opening vernissage dates and has been closed to the public since 9 May, the European Commission confirmed last month that it was terminating its €2m (£1.7m) multiyear grant to the Biennale Foundation.
The row is now also threatening to engulf the Venice film festival, which has a degree of institutional independence from the Biennale but will be directly affected by the funding cut.

The Biennale’s management said the terminated grant used to co-finance the activities of the cinema department relating to Biennale College and the Venice Production Bridge affects “activities and a department that have nothing to do with Russia’s participation in the Biennale Arte”.

In a confrontational speech before the announcement of this year’s lineup, the Biennale’s president, Pietrangelo Buttafuoco, accused the commission of “abandoning our journey”. The Biennale, he said, was not engaged in politics but “international research in the field of arts”.

blocks.caption: The president of the Venice Biennale, Pietrangelo Buttafuoco, has led the criticism of the commission’s decision. Photograph: Stefano Mazzola/Getty Images

blocks.text: For a festival that has in the past often looked more focused on attracting celebrity glitz than its competitors in Cannes and Berlin, this year’s programme is noteworthy for its political flavour and thematic focus on Russia and the countries in its sphere of influence.

As well as Loznitsa’s Imperium, there is the French director Alexandre Smia’s geopolitical “disaster movie” Jupiter, in which the Russian president has survived an assassination attempt for which he blames Ukraine and seeks retribution. Andrei Kutsila’s animated documentary Letters from the Silenced Country focuses on political repression in Belarus, while the Russian-born American film-maker Julia Loktev’s five-hour documentary My Undesirable Friends: Part II – Exile follows a group of Russian dissident journalists working for the independent television channel TV Rain after they are forced to flee their country in the wake of the full-scale invasion.

blocks.caption: My Undesirable Friends: Part II – Exile stars Ksenia Mironova, left, and Valeria Ratnikova. Photograph: Courtesy Venice Film Festival

blocks.text: Loktev’s film circles around the question of where art and journalism stops and propaganda begins. In one scene, the journalists working for TV Rain find themselves chastised for continuing to speak of “our army” after they have registered the network in Latvia. “It’s a film about when your country does terrible things, how to take accountability,” said Loktev. “How do you speak as a citizen of your country about the awful actions and the crimes your country is committing?”

The inclusion of another Russian-themed film project, Ilya Khrzhanovsky’s Dau, has brought criticism from Ukrainian authorities. The Ukrainian ministry of foreign affairs raised “profound concern” over Khrzhanovsky’s film, which tells the story of the Soviet physicist who reluctantly contributed to the creation of the first atomic bomb.

“Russia has long used culture as an instrument of state policy and hybrid warfare,” the ministry said in a statement. “For the Kremlin, culture is a way to restore to sanctioned figures the respectability that politics has taken from them; to legitimise its presence where tanks cannot reach; and to appropriate the history of the very lands it seeks to erase.”
after newsletter promotion

The ministry said that the multi-film Dau project, once described as a “Stalinist Truman Show”, has received funding from the Russian businessman Sergey Adonyev, who has been sanctioned by the US and Ukraine, and that its Greek-born protagonist Teodor Currentzis accepted Russian citizenship granted by Putin.

blocks.caption: A still from Imperium. Photograph: Essential Filmproduktion, Kino Produzioni, Société Parisienne de Production, Studio Uljana Kim - footage courtesy of AAMOD

blocks.text: But in a social media post, the Venice film festival’s artistic director, Alberto Barbera, rejected the description of Dau, which was principally shot from 2008 to 2011, as a “Kremlin-financed project”: “[It] is not a Russian film; it is not pro-Putin propaganda,” he said. “It is a film that denounces totalitarian regimes and their intrusion into citizens’ lives to restrict their freedom.”

Unlike at the Venice art biennial, directors showing their work at the film festival do not represent a country. Dau was funded by Germany, France and Sweden, while My Undesirable Friends was made in the US and Loznitsa’s Imperium has received financial support from Germany, Italy, France and Lithuania.

The comments on the festival row by the Belarus-born, Ukraine-raised and now Germany-based Loznitsa are striking, not least because his own submission to the festival applies a strongly critical lens to the internal contradictions of Russian imperialism, the role of cultural propaganda and blindspots in how the Soviet Union used to be seen from the west – specifically from Italy.

The three-hour film is solely based on archival footage shot by a group of Italian film-makers who, thanks to the blessing of the Italian Communist party, were allowed to make three filming expeditions to the Soviet Union between 1970 and 1973.

blocks.caption: The footage used to make Imperium was shot by Italian film-makers on an officially sanctioned visit. Photograph: Essential Filmproduktion, Kino Produzioni, Société Parisienne de Production, Studio Uljana Kim - footage courtesy of AAMOD

blocks.text: With filming strictly supervised by KGB handlers, the footage they amassed was meant to project the unity of the Soviet empire, showing a sea of red flags on Moscow streets as the patriotic anthem Wide is My Motherland blares from speakers.

Yet the further the crew travels into the outer reaches of the Soviet Union, the more the ambiguous the images become. Local customs, from throat singing to reindeer racing to village wrestling competitions, emphasise the disparity rather than the unity of Soviet culture. In the Yakut Autonomous Soviet Socialist Republic, local people watch on with visible scepticism as a group of urban young Russians parade through the streets with guitars and fiddles.
“I wanted to show that the Soviet Union collapsed not just for economic reasons, but also because it was impossible to keep so many different cultures under one roof,” said Loznitsa.

Moscow’s much-mythologised propaganda arm – still detected by many behind the cultural policies of the Russian state today – appears largely ineffective in Loznitsa’s film. In one scene, the camera hovers over a small tractor parading portraits of members of the politburo through a muddy and forlorn landscape in Dagestan.
“It’s a bit like the Russian pavilion in Venice now,” the film-maker said. “As propaganda, it’s just so ridiculous.”

articles.title: UK must end all trade with Israel, says co-founder of BDS movement
articles.summary:
Exclusive: sanctions against ministers and settler groups are ‘smoke and mirrors cop-out’ says Omar Barghouti

Britain’s legal and ethical obligation to stop a genocide in Gaza requires it to…

blocks.text: Britain’s legal and ethical obligation to stop a genocide in Gaza requires it to take bigger steps than halting trade with illegal Israeli settlements or imposing further sanctions, Omar Barghouti, the co-founder of the Boycott, Divestment, Sanctions (BDS) movement has said.

He described sanctions against individual settler groups or extremist ministers as a “smoke and mirrors cop-out and distraction” from the UK’s legal obligation under international law to end all support for Israel, including arms exports, trade deals and academic relations that “may directly or indirectly enable Israel’s illegal occupation” of Gaza, the West Bank and East Jerusalem.
The British foreign secretary, Ed Miliband, promised on Tuesday to introduce a “comprehensive reset” of the UK’s policy on Israel in the coming weeks.

It has been reported that the UK is preparing to ban trade with illegal Israeli settlements in the West Bank and Miliband told the Commons the government was looking at how to stop British companies “financing, constructing or advertising new settlements”.

Miliband has called plans for the E1 settlement, which would involve the construction of 3,400 houses through the heart of the West Bank, unacceptable and destructive, adding that, by cutting across the territory, critics say it will render a two-state solution impossible.
Tenders for the settlements are due to be handed out, potentially irreversibly, days before the Israeli elections on 27 October.
The Board of Deputies of British Jews and the Jewish Leadership Council have warned Miliband that a UK ban on trade with settlements may fuel antisemitism in the UK.
A third group of British Jews, Yachad, also met Miliband to highlight “the growing concerns of many British Jews about the entrenchment of occupation and effective annexation of the West Bank”.
Barghouti, an influential advocate for Palestinian rights for more than 20 years, said the litmus test for human rights law and the west still lay in Palestine.

He said: “In July 2024, the International Court of Justice (ICJ) said Israel’s entire occupation of Gaza, and the West Bank, including East Jerusalem, is illegal and amounts to a violation of the racial segregation and apartheid prohibitions under international law.
“Dozens of UN human rights experts have said to fulfil those obligations a set of minimal steps are required: a full military embargo, export import, dual-use transfer and transit.
“They also said you have to end all trade, diplomatic and economic relations and academic relations that enable Israel’s illegal occupation.”
Barghouti added: “Further in January 2024, the ICJ said there is a plausible case of the violation of Palestinian rights under the Genocide Convention.

“The ICJ decided there is a plausible risk of genocide that is sufficient to trigger third state responsibilities. But UK government lawyers seem to ignore that part of the ruling and say the court has not ruled on genocide.
“But the genocide convention is very clear – where there is a risk, the obligation to prevent is triggered, and how do you prevent a genocide? You stop enabling it. You end all forms of complicity.”

The Israeli embassy referred to the warning by Gideon Sa’ar, Israel’s foreign minister, who said: “If Britain acts against the state of Israel, the state of Israel will act against Britain. We have the tools.” He added: “The period is over when people act against the state of Israel and the state of Israel doesn’t respond.”
after newsletter promotion
Explaining why he regards UK sanctions as “totally performative”, Barghouti said: “They have no concrete effect in holding Israel to account or pressuring it to comply with international law.”
He added: “Israel has de facto annexed the occupied Palestinian territory, making it near impossible [to] differentiate so-called settlement goods and services.”
Pressed whether the BDS movement is trying to change the minds of Israelis through economic force, Barghouti insisted sanctions have to be legal and ethical.

“They have to target the perpetrators, whether entities or individuals that are involved in crimes, especially international crimes. They are actually measures of accountability, not sanctions that simply say settlers shall not have vacations in London.”

Despite South Africa feeling forced to return to the ICJ to point out Israel is not complying with court orders, he said he retained his faith in international law – for all its colonial origins – arguing it was not something engraved in stone, but dynamic.
“Humanity has agency to evolve and expand international law. We in the BDS movement have been pushing the envelope of its interpretation.”

Barghouti added: “So, in the BDS movement, we try to hold states, corporations and institutions accountable to end their own complicity in genocide rather than just wait for the messiah of international law to come and save us.
“We definitely need international law, just as we need to maintain the ethical high ground. Both are necessary, but not sufficient. We need people power to achieve liberation. There is no other way.”

articles.title: South Korea jails disabled care home head for sexually assaulting residents
articles.summary: The man, surnamed Kim, was handed a 15-year prison term for abusing three residents at the facility near Seoul.

blocks.text: A South Korean court has jailed the former head of a disabled care home for sexually assaulting multiple residents, in a case that shocked the nation.
The man, surnamed Kim, was handed a 15-year prison term for abusing three residents at the Saekdongwon facility in Incheon City, west of Seoul.
Police started investigating Kim after one of his victims, a woman with a severe intellectual disability, came forward in February last year.
The case has prompted the government to inspect 1,507 care facilities for disabled people across the country, where 33 cases of suspected abuse were found.
South Korean Prime Minister Kim Min-seok had described the abuse at Saekdongwon as "a grave matter that calls into question the very reason for the state's existence".
An in-depth assessment of residents commissioned by Ganghwa County found that 20 current and former female residents may have experienced sexual abuse.
Many in South Korea have asked how such a case could still occur, especially after laws were strengthened in 2011 to protect people with disabilities from sexual assault.
Some have also raised questions on how the director's actions could have gone undetected for so long.
Ganghwa County has ordered Saekdongwon to close, while Incheon City officials revoked the licence of the foundation that operated it.
However, the closure has been deferred until the remaining residents have been relocated and arrangements for independent living have been completed.
The foundation has filed an administrative lawsuit challenging the revocation of its licence.

articles.title: Queensland police investigate after 5,500 sheep worth $1.7m stolen from farm
articles.summary:
Police say the sheep were stolen from a property 830km west of Brisbane between February and May

  • Get our breaking…

blocks.text: Queensland police are investigating after about 5,500 Dorper sheep worth more than $1.7m were allegedly stolen from a western Queensland farm.
Police said the sheep were stolen from a property outside Blackall, about 830km west of Brisbane, between February and May this year.
Detective Sen Sgt Paul Elliot, from the rural and stock crime squad, said the sheep had an estimated value of about $1.7m (£899,000).
They are fitted with white National Livestock Identification System tags and are Dorper sheep, a breed with white wool but a black face. Both ewes and rams were taken.
Elliot urged anyone with information about the theft or who had seen Dorper sheep matching the description in the area to come forward.

“Livestock theft investigations can be complex, often spanning large geographical areas, which is why we work closely with producers, saleyards, transport operators and industry stakeholders to identify offenders and disrupt criminal activity,” he said.
The AgForce general president, Shane McCarthy, said it was a “a concerning amount of sheep that have been stolen” and would have a significant effect on the farm’s bottom line.
“We’re seeing a concerning rise in the number of incidents like this happening across the state,” he said. “We would trust that the police are taking these matters very, very seriously.”

He said a sheep theft of that scale would require a plan, time and more than one person. Sheep rustlers will sometimes take a group into a property where they can be bred to gain the value of their progeny and then slowly sold to abattoirs over time.
Thefts are often discovered at the abattoir, he said.

“I would say that it’s been thought out for a while,” he said. “I would suggest that one or two sheep here and there, even up to you know 10 or so sheep, is opportunistic. When we’re talking these numbers, they’re organised.”
It is not yet clear how the sheep were stolen, such as being loaded on to several trucks or mustered.
after newsletter promotion
Dorpers are bred to be eaten, not for wool.
The Blackall-Tambo mayor, Andrew Martin, said the herd was probably not all taken in one night.
“I’m suspecting a number of smaller hits and sneaking them off to the abattoir or whatever it is they’re doing with them,” he said.
Farms in some parts of Queensland can rival the size of some countries. Stock theft is typically discovered during a muster.

Martin, who has farmed Dorper sheep, said some properties have as many as 25,000 sheep. It is possible to lose thousands by them escaping, from an animal attack or just miscounting them, without noticing for a long period of time, he said.
“This is an age-old problem. Potty dodging is a bit of an art, and it’s been going on ever since potties were there to be dodged,” he said, using Australian slang for stock theft.

articles.title: Google launches Pics, its AI-enabled image editor, for Workspace, premium users
articles.summary: Unlike its competitors, Google Pics will let users make written prompts to create images, or have them upload images as a starting point for editing

blocks.text: GOOGLE PICS. Google announces its AI-enabled image generation and editing tool, Google Pics.
Google
Unlike its competitors, Google Pics will let users make written prompts to create images, or have them upload images as a starting point for editing
MANILA, Philippines – Google on Tuesday, September 1, launched a combined image creation and editing tool for Google Workspace and premium users of the company’s suite of tools.

The new offering, Google Pics, is built on its prior Nano Banana offering and will be available as a standalone product as well as becoming part of the company’s Workspace suite, starting with Slides and Docs, and eventually, Drive.

blocks.caption: Google launches Pics, its AI-enabled image editor, for Workspace, premium users

blocks.text: Unlike competitors such as Photoshop, Canva or Adobe Express, Pics will let users make written prompts to create images, or have them upload images as a starting point for editing.

One feature being touted is object segmentation, which lets users isolate an object and transform it without altering other portions of the image. According to Google, “You can input text comments on specific areas to request targeted changes and execute multiple edits at once.”

Further, Google Pics is a collaborative tool, allowing multiple users to edit the same thing at once, It also generates multiple options based on a prompt, so users can take an option built by the AI and run with that iteration or try something new with a different generated option.

Nano Banana was previously in the news following its incorporation into Google Earth. This addition was walked back a few days after launch, after people noted the potential for Nano Banana to make deepfakes of Google Earth images, an unintended use case for the AI tool. Hopefully, this application of the AI image-generation will fare better.

Google Pics is rolling out to Google AI Pro and Ultra subscribers alongside most Workspace business customers. Users can check the Google Pics website for more information on this offering and its availability. – Rappler.com

articles.title: Poa: Purchase of info with confi funds doesn't guarantee success in info gathering
articles.summary: Defense lawyer and former education undersecretary Michael Poa testified Tuesday that purchasing information from informants using confidential funds does not guarantee success in information…

blocks.text: Published September 2, 2026 1:53pm

Defense lawyer and former education undersecretary Michael Poa testified Tuesday that purchasing information from informants using confidential funds does not guarantee success in information gathering.

"Unang-una, hindi kailangan na kapag bumili ka ng information, necessarily, 'pag nakuha mo 'yung information, it will result to success," Poa said when private prosecutor Benjamin Tolosa, Jr. asked if evidence of success is required in the purchase of information as provided under Joint Circular 2015-01, which governs the use of confidential and intelligence funds.
Tolosa cut off Poa after such reply and said "That's my question (only), sir," but Poa insisted on explaining his answer and replied, "Come on, your honor. I'm trying to explain."
Senate impeachment court presiding officer Francis Escudero ruled that Poa should be able to further explain his answer.

Poa then added, "Hindi rin ibig sabihin na at the time na nakuha mo 'yung information and at the time that we needed to submit evidence of success [to the Commission on Audit], necessarily, may success na kaagad."
(It does not mean that just because you already got the information and we needed to submit evidence of success, it does not necessarily mean there is already a success.)

Tolosa then asked asked Poa to confirm that it was his position that the Department of Education (DepEd) paid informants with confidential funds for information, and compliance with 2015 Joint Circular does not necessarily require evidence of success. Poa replied: "Yes, Sir."

Poa also testified that he asked for military certification from then-DepEd undersecretary and retired Colonel Nolasco Mempin to liquidate the department's P15.5 million in confidential funds, and that Mempin did not have personal knowledge on how the P15.5 million in DepEd confidential funds were spent. — VDV, GMA News

articles.title: ‘We have had enough’: thousands of University of Sydney staff walk off the job over AI and job security
articles.summary: Hundreds of university staff were stationed at picket lines, calling for stronger protections around the use of AI

blocks.text: The same week union members at the University of Sydney agreed to a 24-hour strike, staff received the results of an internal survey.
In the faculty of arts and social sciences, 0% agreed with the statement: “I trust the University of Sydney to act in the best interests of staff, students and the broader community.”

It was the issue of trust, alongside longstanding concerns over staff protections from artificial intelligence, workload fairness and job security, that saw about 2,000 members to walk off the job on Wednesday.
From 7am, about 500 people were stationed at picket lines at each of the inner Sydney campus’s entrances, armed with flags, banners and megaphones.
The University of Sydney advised students “almost all” scheduled classes would move online as a result of the strike, while others were rescheduled or cancelled.

Peter Chen, the branch president of the National Tertiary Education Union (NTEU) at the University of Sydney, said management had rebuffed the union “at every opportunity” to enforce appropriate protections around the use of AI.
“Higher education is the canary in the coalmine,” he said. “Where we go on AI … will travel through the rest of the economy.”

The New South Wales division secretary of the NTEU, Vince Caughley, said the University of Sydney’s own green paper advised AI was the most “fundamental transformation” education had seen, pointing to AI chatbots that were already being used to help teach online-only classes at other universities.
“We are asking for best practice, we are asking for due diligence,” he said. “Not their own commercialisation aims and certainly not the interest of venture capital.”

The union was confident it would reach an agreement with management within the year but had concerns over the lack of senior leadership at the table, including the provost, Prof Annamarie Jagose. The last bargaining process represented the longest running industrial action at an Australian university, and the prospect of future strikes remained active.
A spokesperson for the University of Sydney said it was “continuing to engage” with the union and maintained industrial action was “premature”.
“We agree using AI ethically requires a human-centred approach, and our … principles and guardrails that govern use have been developed in consultation with our community,” they said.
“We support many of the objectives of the unions’ claims, but believe it’s more appropriate to implement many of these through relevant policies, instead of in the Enterprise Agreement.”

There are broader concerns, some interlinked and widespread in the sector. Growing class sizes and reduced student satisfaction. A new proposal for teaching-only roles with no research component or scope for future growth.

Prof Laura Shepherd in the school of social and political sciences is part of the bargaining team and said students often sacrificed a “huge amount” to come to the university, including spending $50,000 on degrees.
after newsletter promotion
“They come here … for quality and access to research leaders,” she said. “I think we should be very ashamed if we allow anything in the enterprise agreement that threatens that.”

The University of Sydney’s NTEU branch is the largest in Australia, and the university has long been a hotbed for activism. As management approaches its fifth month of bargaining, it is also grappling with continued opposition to its response to Gaza and restrictions on protest.

New restrictions were brought in as a result of the university’s pro-Palestine encampment in 2024, which received intense scrutiny during this year’s royal commission. On Wednesday, keffiyehs and pro-Palestine banners stood out among purple NTEU flags and signage.

The Student Representative Council was also striking in solidarity with staff and picketing online classes. Its education officer, Dana Kafina, said the university’s “draconian” protest restrictions were a motivation.
“In the wake of … suppressions of free speech and activism, and some of the lowest rates of student and graduate satisfaction in the country, we have had enough,” she said.
Despite the presence of campus security and police, the picket lines had a jovial atmosphere. Some blasted music on speakers, others banged drums and chanted with abandon.
Kurt Iveson, a professor of geography, was among them, running a quiz on his megaphone as, behind him, students sold baked goods to raise funds for lost income of strikers.
Iveson has been with the university for 20 years, and wants “meaningful protections” that do not outlaw AI but ensure “the tech is serving our purpose, rather than us serving the tech”.
“All of us on the picket line today are here because we care so much about the education and research we do,” he said.

articles.title: Modernization program drives higher CSC budget for 2027
articles.summary: In the proposed 2027 budget, P1.45 billion is earmarked for the Civil Service Commission's modernization project. But lawmakers also pressed the CSC to address the high number of contractual…

blocks.text: In the proposed 2027 budget, P1.45 billion is earmarked for the Civil Service Commission's modernization project. But lawmakers also pressed the CSC to address the high number of contractual government workers.

items: The Marcos administration plans to allocate P4.04 billion for the Civil Service Commission in 2027, which is lower than the CSC's original request of P4.81 billion.

The proposed budget includes funding for the Philippine Civil Service Modernization Project, aimed at enhancing human resource capabilities and systems, with a total cost of around P3.88 billion supported by the World Bank.

There are over 1 million contractual workers in the government, and CSC officials are urging a review of policies regarding their employment and the management of job order and contract of service positions.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.
MANILA, Philippines – The Marcos administration is seeking to allocate P4.04 billion for the Civil Service Commission (CSC) next year, based on the 2027 National Expenditure Program (NEP).
The recommended figure, which includes new general appropriations and automatic appropriations, is lower than the CSC’s original proposal of P4.81 billion.

The commission will comply with the Department of Budget and Management’s recommendation, CSC Chairperson Marilyn Barua-Yap told the House appropriations committee during the budget deliberations on Tuesday, September 1.

The 2027 NEP showed the commission’s proposed general fund at P3.89 billion. Broken down, P1.73 billion would go to personnel services, P1.24 billion for maintenance and other operating expenses, and P919 million for capital outlay.
The proposed funding for CSC is 41% higher than the P2.75-billion allocation it received in the 2026 General Appropriations Act, or the national budget.
The increase is due to the allotted P1.45 billion for the Philippine Civil Service Modernization Project (PCSMP), which is a foreign-assisted undertaking.

Yap said the PCSMP aims to strengthen human resource capabilities, modernize human resource systems, and digitize personnel management, making the commission “more responsive, capable, agile, and future-ready.”
For this year, P334 million was earmarked for the PCSMP. Supported by the World Bank, the project costs around P3.88 billion, which runs from 2025 to 2029.

The World Bank previously said the project would establish the Human Resources Management Information System and payroll system to “improve analytics for workforce planning, career development, succession planning, and training.” It also sets up a human resource certification system to “standardize and increase the competence of human resource management officers.”
Here are the proposed amounts for other CSC programs:

items: Civil Service Professionalization and Workplace Cooperation Program – P726 million
Administrative Justice Program – P197 million
Civil Service Human Resource Governance Program – P72 million

blocks.text: The Career Executive Service Board, which is attached to the CSC, is seeking P143 million for 2027.
But some lawmakers pressed the CSC on how it would address the high number of contractual workers in the government workforce.
Yap said there are more than 3 million government workers, including 2 million career professionals and around 1 million workers with only job orders (JO) and contracts of service (COS).

CSC Commissioner Ryan Acosta said the national government agencies with the highest number of contractual workers were the Department of Public Works and Highways, Department of Education, Department of Health, Department of Social Welfare and Development, and Department of Environment and Natural Resources.
During the budget briefing, Acosta said many of the contractual workers in these agencies are involved in the distribution of welfare benefits.
He said around 70% of the JO and COS workers were in the local governments.

Acosta urged the Department of the Interior and Local Government to study whether a rigid personal services limitation on local government funding remains relevant and whether a cap on the number of their JO and COS workers must be implemented.
The commissioner urged Congress to carefully review present laws that create mandatory positions without regard to the needs and capacities of LGUs, particularly low-income communities.
He said the DBM should relax its scrap and build policy, a strategy where agencies abolish obsolete or vacant positions to create new positions or units.

Acosta also recommended that the proposed optimization committee explore the possibility of having trigger points in reviewing agencies that repeatedly hire JO and COS workers for the same position for a number of years.

Yap said it is the responsibility of the agency to maintain and update its inventory of their JO and COS workers as they are not covered by the CSC. Data collected may be used to craft policies to improve the welfare of contractual workers.

“We will always welcome any initiative to support benefits for the JO and COS [workers], but it is unfortunate that we cannot guarantee their absorption into the civil service as of this time,” she said. – Rappler.com

articles.title: Wednesday briefing: ​What’s behind the global backlash against datacentres?
articles.summary: In today’s newsletter: Communities from Scotland to India are pushing back against datacentres they feel have been forced upon them, warning they threaten energy supplies and the…

blocks.text: Good morning. This summer, datacentres have become targets of resistance across the world. Ever since the arrival of ChatGPT, big tech has been lobbying for the creation of enormous new facilities. Many governments claim they’re essential in any country that wants to cash in on AI.

Campaigners argue datacentres drain resources and exacerbate the climate crisis. The Scottish National Party has backed a moratorium on new developments; so has the Greens. The boom has been immense, and so has the backlash. Today’s newsletter explains why.

At First Edition, we’re keen on pushing the boundaries of frontier technologies (no luddites here), so today we’re trying something new: we’ve produced a video to accompany this newsletter, which you can watch on the Guardian’s Instagram page. Let us know what you think by replying to this email. How’s that for innovation? Before you do, here are the headlines.
Five big stories

items: UK politics | Andy Burnham has blamed Brexit and Margaret Thatcher for a decade of low growth in the UK, arguing that Britain needs to be brutally honest about having taken “a series of wrong turns” in the last 40 years.
Nepal-Tibet | A week on from the flash flooding disaster, authorities are urging relatives of the thousands of missing and dead to provide blood samples.

Middle East | The US has launched new airstrikes on Iranian targets, prompting counter strikes by Tehran targeting American interests in Bahrain, Kuwait, Jordan and Iraq, fuelling concerns about a ⁠wider renewal of hostilities.
Ukraine | Russia has opened a deadly new phase in its war against Ukraine by deliberately targeting the country’s railway network, with six employees killed on Tuesday in the latest strikes on Kyiv.
US news | Mark Carney has rebuked Donald Trump’s administration and urged officials in Washington to “start being serious” amid escalation trade tensions between the US and Canada.

blocks.text: In depth: ‘We’re in an extremely anti-democratic moment with AI’

blocks.caption: Campaigners trying to prevent a new AI datacentre planned for the old Truman Brewery in Brick Lane. Photograph: David Levene/The Guardian

blocks.text: In August I attended a meeting of campaigners and councillors in the east London borough of Tower Hamlets, where the government has recently approved plans for a 5,200 sq mile datacentre on the site of an old brewery off Brick Lane. The meeting, held on a sunny Monday evening, went on for three hours, in a stifling hall so packed that organisers had to create an overflow room. It’s a testament to how divisive the subject has become.

The new east London datacentre won’t be anywhere near as large as the “hyperscale” datacentres that power AI, which are typically 10,000 square feet or more. Neither is it the first to be built in the area (there are already three similarly sized developments nearby). But attenders I spoke with shared the same concerns as other campaign groups globally. They worried about the amount of energy the building will consume (5.2MW, according to a local campaign group, which is enough to power 15,000 homes), about its use of water (projections for this haven’t been released), and about the noise and heat it could emit.

They have good reasons to be concerned. The IMF estimates that by 2030, datacentres will consume more energy than all but the world’s three largest state emitters (China, India and the United States). They are already driving up electricity prices: one analysis found that wholesale electricity prices rose 267% over five years in locations near datacentres in Virginia. And although the industry argues that technology in newer AI datacentres consume less water than older facilities, not even the Environment Agency knows how much water datacentres use. It’s one of many unknowns.

Much of the anger here centres on how it’s been approved. Despite fierce opposition from local residents and Tower Hamlets council, which wants the site to be used for hundreds of homes, housing secretary Angela Rayner intervened, overruling the council to approve the application, citing its creation of 44 homes (only six of which will be socially rented) as a “significant” public benefit.

“When you have Andy Burnham talking about devolution and democracy, this feels like a slap in the face,” Henna Khanom, a Tower Hamlets resident, told me. “To me, it feels like many of these are springing up in places where low-income, ethnic minority communities just don’t have the power to resist these changes.”
This reflects a feature common to many of these battles: locals feel that datacentres are being forced on them against their will, with very little transparency or democratic oversight.
How many datacentres exist?

Globally, the number of “hyperscale” datacentres has nearly tripled since 2018. The UK had 52 datacentres in 2000, and today there are an estimated 520, roughly 48 of which are “hyperscale”, though it’s impossible to get exact figures, since nobody (not even the government) knows the total number that have been built. In the US, where local governments have signed NDAs with tech companies, information is shielded from scrutiny. In the EU, Microsoft and other American tech companies successfully lobbied to conceal the environmental impact of their developments.

Secrecy is power, particularly when your industry devours massive amounts of energy, much of it powered by fossil fuels. Because developers can wait years for an electricity grid connection, many are now opting to build their own gas-fired power plants instead. In the UK, more than 100 datacentres intend to burn gas to generate their electricity. It’s possible that some may do this permanently. These are reasons you might expect more scrutiny of these developments, not less.

“We’re in an extremely anti-democratic moment with AI,” the Guardian’s tech correspondent Aisha Down tells me. It’s no wonder, then, that so many protests are kicking off. Several weeks ago, police in Scotland warned one developer that public anger over these buildings was so great it now poses a security risk.
Why does the government want more of them?

The Starmer government tended to proselytise about the benefits of big tech. In documents outlining the UK’s AI strategy last year, it argued that datacentres were “the engines of the AI age”, and set out its plans to accelerate construction. So far, Burnham’s government seems to agree: last week, he rejected the Green party’s proposal for a moratorium on new developments, arguing this would “send investment and good jobs abroad”.

Since the start of this year, the government has allowed datacentres to opt into Nationally Significant Infrastructure Projects (NSIPS), where the secretary of state rather than local councils make planning decisions, enabling developers to bypass local scrutiny. Two of the first datacentres to opt into the NSIPs scheme are applying to build new private gas power stations to fire up their operations, which will together be responsible for more than 4.5m tonnes of carbon emissions. “Most people don’t want diesel generators running constantly near where they live,” Aisha says. “That sort of thing is upsetting to communities.”
What are they good for?

With all the recent attention on datacentres, it’s worth noting many have existed for years, quietly whirring away and processing information you need to send emails or read newsletters like this one. Clearly, we need some datacentres. The question is whether we need the “hyperscale” variety.

There has been lots of noise among policymakers about the UK being an “AI maker, not an AI taker” that can’t afford to be left behind in the AI “race” or lose its AI “sovereignty.” But nobody seems to agree on exactly how datacentres achieves these vague aims. Will they rejuvenate post-industrial areas with shiny new jobs? Probably not. Will they help the UK “shape the AI revolution”? It’s hard to see precisely how, when US tech companies building many of the datacentres on UK soil retain control over infrastructure, IP and profits. “People in the highest echelons of power seem to be making policy based on AI Fomo and vibes,” Aisha says.

We’ll return to this vibes-based strategy and the risky financing of the AI boom in future newsletters. For now, it’s clear these fights reflect a feeling that datacentres are something done to communities, regardless of whether they consent. The Burnham government hopes to reignite people’s faith in democracy by giving them more control. The battle over datacentres will be a major test of that commitment.

articles.title: OVP seeks P785.204M budget for 2027
articles.summary: The Office of the Vice President (OVP) has proposed a P785.204-million budget for 2027, 11.7% lower than its P889.236-million appropriated budget for 2026.

blocks.text: Published September 2, 2026 1:43pm
The Office of the Vice President (OVP) has proposed a P785.204-million budget for 2027, 11.7% lower than its P889.236-million appropriated budget for 2026.
In a statement on Wednesday, the OVP said this year’s budget aims to support the agency’s continued delivery of assistance and services to beneficiaries nationwide.
The 2027 budget recommendation includes P220.232 million for Personnel Services (PS), P561.651 million for Maintenance and Other Operating Expenses (MOOE), and P3.321 million for Capital Outlay.
Meanwhile, P15.544 million is automatically appropriated for the Retirement and Life Insurance Premium (RLIP) of OVP plantilla personnel.
The OVP also noted its consistent high budget utilization rate, averaging over 90% in recent years.
As of June 30, the agency reported a 43.07% obligation rate for its 2026 budget, surpassing its 41% target.
The OVP said a large part of its MOOE budget will fund the agency’s programs that give assistance to individuals, families, commuters, learners, and communities.

Of the total MOOE budget, P193.103 million is allocated for the procurement of goods and the provision of livelihood assistance grants under the OVP’s MagNegosyo Ta ‘Day program, as well as other assistance and service-oriented initiatives.
Among the programs identified for funding are:
• Pagbabago Campaign — targeting 150,000 learners;
• Disaster Operations — targeting 23,000 individuals/families;
• R.I.I.C.E. Food Bags — targeting 30,000 individuals/families;
• Libreng Sakay — targeting 1.2 million commuters;
• KALUSUGAN Food Truck and Disaster Operations
• Wheelchair Distribution
• Al-Janazah Kits and Other Supplies; and
• You Can Be VP Program

“The OVP remains committed to ensuring that available public funds are directed toward essential services and programs that provide meaningful assistance to Filipinos, while maintaining prudent and responsible spending in the implementation of its mandate,” the agency said.
The national budget for 2027 is P7.2 trillion, which is 6% higher than the P6.793 trillion budget in 2026. — RSJ, GMA News

articles.title: Nepal, Philippines suffer greatly despite contributing little to climate crisis
articles.summary: There is consensus that climate change is caused by industrialized nations, and poorer countries have time and again demanded for reparations

blocks.text: There is consensus that climate change is caused by industrialized nations, and poorer countries have time and again demanded for reparations
MANILA, Philippines – Developing nations like Nepal and the Philippines bear the brunt of climate change impacts even though they contribute the least to global greenhouse gas emissions.

Nepal is suffering from the debris flow and massive flood triggered by a glacier collapse in the Himalayas, and the death toll continues to rise. In the Philippines, millions have had to grapple with flooded roads and homes due to continuous rain in recent weeks.

“We contribute a negligible share of global emissions, yet we sit downstream of some of the fastest-warming glacial systems on Earth,” Sumnima Udas, a member of the Nepal parliament, was quoted as saying in a The New Yorker report.
There is consensus that climate change is caused mainly by industrialized nations. Poorer countries vulnerable to climate change impacts have time and again demanded for reparations.
Last year, the International Court of Justice ruled in a landmark opinion that responsible countries “have an obligation to compensate.” – Rappler.com
Reporter, editor, writer: Iya Gozum

articles.title: Gov't approves first commercially available ASF vaccine
articles.summary: The Bureau of Animal Industry (BAI) has approved the commercial sale of AVAC ASF LIVE, the first African swine fever (ASF) vaccine available for fatteners, or pigs raised for pork production.

blocks.text: Published September 2, 2026 1:38pm
The Bureau of Animal Industry (BAI) has approved the commercial sale of AVAC ASF LIVE, the first African swine fever (ASF) vaccine available for fatteners, or pigs raised for pork production.
According to the Department of Agriculture (DA), AVAC ASF LIVE was developed by AVAC Vietnam Joint Stock Company.

“The availability of a commercially approved ASF vaccine is crucial to our repopulation program. It gives hog raisers another tool to protect healthy animals as we work to rebuild the industry and secure a more stable supply of pork,” DA Secretary Francisco Tiu Laurel Jr. said in a statement.
ASF first hit the Philippines in 2019, reducing the country’s hog population from 13 million heads to around 8 million. The BAI has reported ASF outbreaks in 76 of the country’s 82 provinces.
Agriculture Undersecretary for Livestock Constante Palabrica said a second vaccine, South Korea’s PROVAC, is currently being evaluated by the BAI.

Palabrica also asked Tiu Laurel for P1 billion in the proposed 2027 budget to subsidize ASF vaccination for backyard pig farms, potentially making the vaccine more accessible to small-scale producers.

The DA recently issued a circular lifting the temporary ban on the importation of industrially manufactured, hermetically sealed and heat-treated canned pork products imposed due to the threat of ASF.
The department said its risk analysis conducted in January showed that the biosecurity risks associated with the products were negligible.

The World Organisation for Animal Health’s Terrestrial Animal Health Code provides that heat treatment of at least 30 minutes at a minimum temperature of 70 degrees Celsius can inactivate the ASF virus in meat.— MCG, GMA News
