articles.summary: TARLAC CITY – President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. on Wednesday inspected the ongoing construction of a Bailey bridge to restore access to the collapsed 136-meter-long Agana Bridge here following…

blocks.text: TARLAC CITY – President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. on Wednesday inspected the ongoing construction of a Bailey bridge to restore access to the collapsed 136-meter-long Agana Bridge here following extreme rains and river movement over the weekend.

Together with Public Works Secretary Vivencio Dizon, the President directed the Department of Public Works and Highways to fast-track the construction of the alternate bridge and said the government will provide P300 million in assistance to the Tarlac City government for its rehabilitation.

Marcos said the type of damage incurred by Agana Bridge at Barangay Tibag, which motorists use to access the towns of Sta. Ignacia, Mayantoc, Camiling and San Clemente, as well as the August 28 destruction of the 720-meter-long Aquino Bridge, were the consequences of climate change.
Accompanying the President in the inspection were Tarlac City Mayor Susan Yap, Tarlac Gov. Christian Yap, and Tarlac Rep. Cristy Angeles.
Mayor Yap said they need 10 days to finish the Bailey bridge construction and to conduct a stress test, but only light vehicles will be allowed to pass Agana bridge.

On Aug 29, an SUV fell into the Tarlac River right when the Agana bridge collapsed. Only one of the five passengers survived. The remains of two passengers were recovered in Pangasinan, while the last 2 passengers remain missing.
Tarlac was placed under a state of calamity on August 30 following the massive damage from the southwest monsoon. /coa

articles.title: Hopes of finding survivors dim a week after catastrophic Nepal flood
articles.summary: At least 1,050 people have been killed and nearly 4,000 remain unaccounted for, with officials fearing many are buried under debris left by the floods that tore through towns and valleys near the…

blocks.text: RETRIEVAL OPERATIONS. Army rangers carry a victim airlifted from an area affected by flash floods and a mudslide at Maithili Barrack, an army training centre, in Trishuli, Nuwakot District, Nepal, September 2, 2026.
Francis Mascarenhas/REUTERS

At least 1,050 people have been killed and nearly 4,000 remain unaccounted for, with officials fearing many are buried under debris left by the floods that tore through towns and valleys near the Chinese border

KATHMANDU, Nepal – Hopes of finding more survivors among the thousands still missing in Nepal were fading, authorities said on Wednesday, September 2, a week after a glacier collapse in the Himalayas unleashed flash floods that devastated the mountainous nation.

At least 1,050 people have been killed and nearly 4,000 remain unaccounted for, with officials fearing many are buried under debris left by the floods that tore through towns and valleys near the Chinese border.
Across the border in Tibet, China’s official toll has held steady since Sunday at 16 dead and 546 missing.
“The hope of finding survivors is decreasing,” Phanindra Paudel, a senior official at the government’s National Emergency Operation Center (NEOC), said. “We pray and are hopeful. Hope is hope!”

Rescuers are trying to find survivors believed to be trapped inside the tunnels of several hydroelectric plants, whose powerhouses have spaces and rooms for people to stay, army spokesperson Raja Ram Basnet said.
Authorities said 279 people had been rescued from the ruins of hydropower projects but at least 639 more were still missing, some of whom are believed to be trapped in tunnels.

“Looking at the nature of the disaster and the area which has been hit by the flood, as days go by there are less chances of human survivors,” Binoj Basnet, a retired senior army general who oversaw the search and rescue operation during the 2015 earthquake in which about 9,000 people were killed, said.
Prime Minister Balendra Shah said the focus would shift from search, rescue and relief operations towards rehabilitation and reconstruction.

“The government is now focusing on rehabilitation while working to protect the lives of people in the affected areas and providing necessary medical treatment and psychological counselling,” Shah said in a late-night post on social media on Tuesday, September 1.

The disaster left at least 2.2 million tons of debris, according to a preliminary estimate by the United Nations Development Programme (UNDP), including parts of buildings, rocks, and sediment, the equivalent of six Empire State buildings.
“The amount of debris shows the scale of the destruction and the challenge communities face as they clear homes, roads, and public spaces and begin to rebuild,” it said.

UN spokesperson Stephane Dujarric said aid agencies were “very concerned” about the growing public health risk from overcrowded shelters, contaminated water and damaged health facilities, particularly for women and children during the monsoon season.

About 3,900 people remain unaccounted for and nearly 3,500 people are living in 27 displacement sites across the hardest-hit districts of Nuwakot and Rasuwa, Dujarric told a regular UN press briefing on Tuesday.
Shah said his government had stepped up surveillance and response measures to prevent possible outbreaks of disease in flood-affected areas.
The Himalayan region faces severe risks from future glacial floods, a senior UN official said on Tuesday, a sentiment that Shah echoed in his post.
“Questions about why the ice and rock collapsed and how such a large volume of water was generated must be answered by the global community,” Shah said.
China has linked the flood to climate change as well. – Rappler.com

articles.title: Japan halves speed limit to 30km/h on all narrow city streets
articles.summary:
Speed limit dropped from 60km/h for around 70% of general roads in the hope of making narrow streets of crowded cities safer

Drivers on residential roads in

blocks.text: Drivers on residential roads in Japan have been forced to take their foot off the accelerator, after the speed limit was slashed from 60km/h (37mph) to 30km/h in an attempt to reduce deaths and injuries among pedestrians on narrow urban streets.
The new limit, which went into effect on Tuesday, applies to residential roads with no centre line or maximum speed signs, media reports said.

Narrow roads with no centre lines or pavements are a common sight in crowded Japanese cities, with data indicating that children and older people are at particular risk of being involved in a fatal or serious accident.

The measures apply to about 870,000km of roads that are less than 5.5 metres wide and do not have centre lines or median strips, according to the Mainichi Shimbun. They account for about 70% of the country’s general roads, the newspaper said.
Authorities hopes the restrictions will address concerns that residential areas are not experiencing the same improvements in safety seen on larger roads.

While the overall number of deaths in traffic accidents is in decline – falling to a record low of 2,457 last year – those involving children and older people on residential roads has remained steady at about 300 a year since 2021, and rose for the first time in three years in 2025, according to the national police agency.
The introduction in 2011 of “zone 30” areas on a limited number of residential streets and along school routes resulted in a 30% reduction in fatalities and serious injuries, the Mainichi said.

Police agency data show that the mortality rate among pedestrians is less than 1% in accidents involving vehicles traveling at or below 30km/h, with the rate rising to 2.7% at speeds of 30-40km/h, and to 17.4% at 50-60km/h.

“We ask drivers to recognise that they need to take particular care on roads shared by vehicles, pedestrians and cyclists,” the police agency’s commissioner general, Yoshinobu Kusunoki, told reporters this week.

articles.title: Israel expanding presence in Lebanon, officials say, as BBC visits occupied areas
articles.summary: A BBC team joined a humanitarian mission of the UN peacekeeping force, which says Israeli troops are fortifying positions and continuing demolitions.

blocks.text: Israel expanding presence in Lebanon, officials say, as BBC visits occupied areas
Watch: BBC sees Israeli military presence in southern Lebanon
By
Middle East correspondentReporting fromsouthern Lebanon

The drive on the highway by the Mediterranean in southern Lebanon, near the border with Israel, is scenic and, these days, desolate. Crops lie abandoned and buildings destroyed by Israeli air strikes, too many to count, are in ruins.

Near the town of Naqoura, a Lebanese military checkpoint, painted in the white-and-red colours of the national flag, is the last visible sign of the state's presence. Soldiers are positioned behind concrete walls, but the road is empty. A few minutes further south, around a dozen Israeli flags indicate the start of occupied territory. Unless authorised by Israel, no-one can enter.

This part of the country is the heartland of Lebanon's Shia Muslim community, from which Hezbollah, the Iranian-backed militia and political party, gets most of its support. It has seen three invasions by the Israeli military in wars against the group in the last two decades alone. The most recent started in March, after Hezbollah fired rockets into Israel following the killing of the Iranian supreme leader, at the start of the US and Israel's war against Iran.

Last month, a BBC team joined a humanitarian mission of the UN peacekeeping force in Lebanon, known as Unifil, which is one of the only ways to visit the area under Israeli control. There, as it did in Gaza, Israel has flattened entire villages, and air strikes and demolitions have continued even after a ceasefire was announced in June.

blocks.caption: Image caption, An Israeli soldier at a checkpoint established in a residential building near the Unifil headquarters in Naqoura

blocks.text: Image source, Neha Sharma/BBC
An Israeli soldier at a checkpoint established in a residential building near the Unifil headquarters in Naqoura

Led by Finnish troops who are part of Unifil, the convoy was escorting civilians to and from Christian villages near the border. Those communities were spared from Israel's attacks and invasion during the war and, with the surrounding areas now under occupation, are now cut off from the rest of the country. Our presence was allowed by the Israeli military through a deconfliction mechanism with the UN.

The strip of land currently controlled by Israel constitutes around 5% of Lebanese territory and, in some places, extends 10km (six miles) from the border. Driving along the wall that separates the two countries, we saw service roads built by Israel after the invasion, intense movement of Israeli soldiers and residential buildings that were being used by them. Some were covered in netting to protect them from Hezbollah's explosive drones.
We also heard Israeli surveillance drones in the sky and explosions in the distance, possibly from demolitions being carried out by Israel in villages that are under occupation.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Israeli soldiers drive on a road along the wall separating Lebanon and Israel

blocks.text: Israeli soldiers drive on a road along the wall separating Lebanon and Israel

In a visit to occupied southern Lebanon last month, Israeli Defence Minister Israel Katz said he had instructed the military to "take all necessary steps to prepare for a long-term presence in the area". Israeli officials say their goal is to establish what they call a "security zone" to protect communities in northern Israel from rockets and drones that have been fired by Hezbollah from southern Lebanon, as well as a possible ground invasion.

According to Unifil, the Israeli military has established four new bases in the invaded areas, bringing the number of such positions to nine. Israeli forces had remained in five points after invading southern Lebanon during the previous war against Hezbollah in 2024, in violation of the deal that ended that conflict.

"In the past months, we've seen the consolidation and fortification of Israeli positions, construction of protective infrastructure, and other engineering works," Kandice Ardiel, a Unifil spokeswoman, said. "We have [also] observed what appear to be Israeli civilian personnel carrying out demolition and engineering activities in support of military activities in south Lebanon."

Human rights groups say some of Israel's actions in southern Lebanon amount to the deliberate destruction of civilian infrastructure, a possible war crime. Hundreds of thousands of Lebanese remain displaced, without knowing when, or if, they will be able to return.

In response to our questions, the Israeli military said the buildings that had been destroyed were used by Hezbollah for military purposes, and that it operated in accordance with international law. It did not respond to other specific questions about its actions in the occupied areas.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Some of the houses used by the Israeli military are covered in netting to protect them from Hezbollah's explosive drones

blocks.text: Some of the houses used by the Israeli military are covered in netting to protect them from Hezbollah's explosive drones

In June, the US and Iran announced a preliminary deal aimed at ending their conflict, which included a cessation of the violence in Lebanon. Since then, a Lebanese intelligence official told me, Lebanon's military has recorded more than 5,000 violations of the deal by Israel, including air strikes, drone attacks, shelling and near-daily incursions of Israeli soldiers into Lebanese territory beyond the area under occupation, the so-called Yellow Line.

As it does in Gaza, the Israeli military justifies some of its attacks in Lebanon as operations against what it describes as immediate threats. In many cases, however, it is not clear how immediate these alleged threats are or if there is any threat at all. Hezbollah, which is considered a terrorist organisation by countries including the UK and the US, has not carried out attacks against Israel since the ceasefire came into force, but has targeted Israeli troops operating inside Lebanese territory.

"[The Israelis] are expanding their presence [in Lebanon]. They've [also] been setting areas ablaze, demolishing houses while the bombing continues, despite the ceasefire," the Lebanese intelligence official said. "It's clear that they don't want anyone to go back [to those villages] in the coming year, or even years. This isn't only about Hezbollah. This is about preventing people from returning."

blocks.caption: Image caption, Entire villages along the border have been destroyed by Israel

blocks.text: Entire villages along the border have been destroyed by Israel

Israeli officials have conditioned a withdrawal from Lebanon on Hezbollah's disarmament, something the Lebanese government cannot deliver without the group's consent. Hezbollah, observers say, is still a significant military force despite the setbacks in the recent wars. Both countries have held direct talks that resulted in a framework agreement brokered by the US: Israel would pull out of certain areas, called "pilot zones", where Lebanese army soldiers would be deployed and Hezbollah's disarmament would be verified.

Hezbollah opposes the efforts – the group's leader, Naim Qassem, called them "surrender with humiliation" last week – and says any discussion about its weapons should only happen after a full Israeli withdrawal. Israel, for its part, has claimed that the Lebanese national military, which rejects the use of force against the group saying this could pit Lebanese against Lebanese, has not done enough.
The plan has seen no progress, and there is no expectation of any significant change before the Israeli election at the end of October.

"The idea of the 'pilot zones' seems to be dead until the context changes," a European diplomat familiar with the situation told me. "It seems we're heading to a Gaza-like situation. The Israelis are entrenching themselves... and are here to stay, for now."

articles.title: Jury in Bruce Lehrmann’s Queensland rape trial may face questions about prior knowledge of case
articles.summary:
Lehrmann is accused of raping a woman in 2021 and will stand trial in Toowoomba in November. He intends to contest the charges

  • Get our

blocks.text: Jurors in the pending trial of Bruce Lehrmann for alleged rape could be questioned about their prior knowledge of him and the case.
Lehrmann, 31, is set to stand trial from 2 November, accused of twice raping a woman at a house in regional Queensland in 2021.
Lehrmann’s case was mentioned in Toowoomba district court on Wednesday to list any pre-trial applications.
Prosecutor Caroline Marco said she intended to file an application under a part of Queensland’s Jury Act.
Marco said she was bringing the application as it appeared Lehrmann was seeking a jury trial.
Section 47 of the Jury Act allows for jury members to be questioned if a judge determines there are “special reasons”.
“Prejudicial pre-trial publicity may be a special reason for questioning persons selected as jurors or reserve jurors in the final stage of the jury selection process,” the act states.
If the prosecutor is granted a section 47 inquiry, they can suggest questions to be asked of jury members, but the judge will have final say.
If a judge considers further inquiry is justified, the defence and prosecution could also be allowed to cross-examine jurors under oath.
Jury members could be discharged in response to the answers they give and replaced with another person from a pool of potential jurors before the trial starts.
Those replacements can also be questioned.
Marco said she would file her application in the next few days.
after newsletter promotion
Defence solicitor Zali Burrows was not required to respond to the prosecution’s intent to file an application.
Lehrmann has not formally entered a plea but his previous legal counsel has told a magistrate he intends to contest the charges.
Judge Dennis Lynch adjourned the matter for two weeks to allow the prosecution and defence to file further material.
Lehrmann was not required to appear in court on Wednesday and his bail was continued.

articles.title: Prosecution, defense teams clash over supposed insult vs Poa
articles.summary: MANILA, Philippines — The direct examination of Michael Poa as one of the prosecution’s hostile witnesses in Vice President Sara Duterte’s impeachment trial got off to a rough start after the defense…

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines — The direct examination of Michael Poa as one of the prosecution’s hostile witnesses in Vice President Sara Duterte’s impeachment trial got off to a rough start after the defense accused the prosecution of “insulting” the defense lawyer.
During the 21st day of Duterte’s impeachment, the prosecution presented Poa, who is a part of the defense counsel, as a witness.

In offering Poa’s testimony, private prosecutor Benjamin Tolosa Jr. noted several times that it was Poa who responded to the Commission on Audit’s (COA) audit observation memorandum regarding DepEd’s use of confidential funds, despite him claiming of “knowing absolutely nothing about” it.

“The Vice President chose him, the man who knew nothing, to answer the auditors. Sa kabila noon, siya ang inatasan ng bise presidente sumagot sa COA, hindi ang SDO (special disbursing officer), hindi ang nag-disburse ng pera, hindi ang tumanggap ng pera—ang abogadong walang alam,” said Tolosa.

(The Vice President chose him, the man who knew nothing, to answer the auditors. Despite that, he was the one the Vice President appointed to answer the COA, not the SDO, not the one who disbursed the money, not the one who received the money—the lawyer who knew nothing.)
Defense lead counsel Sheila Sison objected to the remark and asked the court to strike out the phrase “abogadong walang alam,” tagging it as “improper.”

“This witness (Poa), even while he has an obligation to answer relevant questions in this trial. He also has, under Rules 132, certain rights, and one of those rights is to be protected from irrelevant, improper and insulting questions,” said Sison.
“Not only that but also to be protected from harsh and insulting demeanor,” she added.
Tolosa, for his part, clarified that he had no intention of insulting Poa.

“We have to take this in context, when I said ang ‘abogadong walang alam,’ what I meant was in Congress he repeatedly said he knew totally nothing about the use and liquidation of the confidential funds. Context is very important,” said Tolosa.
“But nonetheless if I offended you in any way, that’s not my intention,” he added.

But Sison retorted that that if this was the point Tolosa wanted to portray, he could have simply said “the witness has no personal knowledge,” which to her would have been “more respectful and appropriate.”
“I am certain that the counsel has in his vocabulary other terms,” said Sison.
Court presiding officer and Senator-judge Francis “Chiz” Escudero ruled to strike the line off the record, stating that he himself found it discourteous.
“[It] should not be used in relation to a fellow lawyer, especially,” said Escudero. /jpv

articles.title: Psychologist warns against mental health stigma amid school violence
articles.summary: MANILA, Philippines — A psychologist warned against the stigmatization of mental health conditions amid recent reports of school violence. “Maaaring nakakaramdam ang isang tao ng ganito. May…

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines — A psychologist warned against the stigmatization of mental health conditions amid recent reports of school violence.

“Maaaring nakakaramdam ang isang tao ng ganito. May depression siya. May anxiety siya. Nakakaisip ng mga negative thoughts. Pero, hindi naman necessarily magta-translate yan to school violence,” Dr. John Manuel Kliatchko, president of the Psychologists Association of the Philippines, said at the Kapihan sa Manila Prince Hotel on Wednesday.
(A person may have depression, anxiety and negative thoughts, but this doesn’t necessarily translate to school violence.)
“Hindi natin dapat inii-stigmatize yung ganoon,” he stressed.
(We should not stigmatize mental health conditions.)
Instead, Kliatchko advocated for the presence of “responsible adults.”
“Malaki sana ang mape-prevent natin when it comes to these,” he added.
(We would prevent a lot when it comes to these.)

The mental well-being of children and adolescents became a subject of public discussions following the fatal shooting incidents in Tacloban City on June 22 and Zamboanga City on August 18, both allegedly carried out by teenage gunmen.

Although investigators did not find any incidents of bullying against the perpetrator in the Zamboanga case, the police previously said the gunmen in the Tacloban case had reportedly been bullied beforehand.

“Katulad ng pagkakaroon ng access to weapons, hindi naman yan naiisip ng isang bata, or nagpaplano na or nagbabasa ng mga material, sa Youtube, for example, nanonood na siya kung paano gumawa ng bomba,” Kliatchko explained.
(Similar to getting access to weapons, a child wouldn’t think of that or of planning an attack or reading materials, watching tutorials to make a bomb on YouTube.)
“Hindi naman yan maiisip ng isang taong may mental condition dahil lamang sa kanyang mental health condition,” he added.
(A person with a mental condition wouldn’t think of those things simply because of his mental health condition.)

The Philippine National Police (PNP) previously reported that it recorded at least 50 incidents of school violence involving children in conflict with the law from the beginning of School Year 2026–2027 in June to mid-August. /jpv

articles.title: TB medicine supplies may arrive by October, DOH says
articles.summary: MANILA, Philippines – Tuberculosis (TB) medication supplies may arrive as early as next month, acting Health Secretary Edwin Mercado said on Wednesday. Mercado acknowledged that the agency had faced…

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines – Tuberculosis (TB) medication supplies may arrive as early as next month, acting Health Secretary Edwin Mercado said on Wednesday.

Mercado acknowledged that the agency had faced procurement delays for anti-TB medicines and testing cartridges, as he urged the Department of Health (DOH) to fast-track the purchase of essential drugs and equipment.
The agency is set to evaluate bids from Sept. 3 to 10, with contracts expected to be awarded by the end of the month, he said. Supplies could be delivered as early as October or November.
“I gave a directive to really push,” Mercado told lawmakers.
TB is an endemic illness in the Philippines, which ranked third globally in 2024 after the country accounted for 6.8 percent of cases worldwide, according to a 2025 World Health Organization report.
The DOH implements a national TB control program, and Mercado’s predecessor, Jose Brittanio “Brix” Pujalte, Jr. came under fire for allegedly delaying the medicine’s procurement.
Pujalte denied the claim, saying the review was for transparency and to ensure the purchase complies with government regulations.
Mercado also said the DOH sought a foreign grant worth almost $159 million for TB, malaria and human immunodeficiency virus medicine, though he gave no further details. /dl

articles.title: British man deported from Sweden despite living there since childhood
articles.summary:
John Sellers, 34, who moved with his family to Sweden aged 10, has been ejected despite his recent marriage to a Swede

A 34-year-old British man who has lived in Sweden since he was 10 has…

blocks.text: A 34-year-old British man who has lived in Sweden since he was 10 has been deported in the latest of a series of Brexit-induced catastrophes for UK citizens in the country.
John Sellers was told to leave despite living in Sweden for 24 years, having been educated in the country and newly married to his Swedish partner, Caroline.
“It is time people know how people are being treated here, and it is time to show what Brexit has caused,” he said, as he described his near seven-year struggle to remain in the country.

“Quite frankly, we have been holding our tongues too long. I am very well aware that different countries have different rules on immigration, but none of this would have happened were it not for Brexit,” he said.

His parents moved to Sweden from Essex under the free movement rights that came with the UK’s membership of the EU because they liked the education system and thought it was a “good place to bring up children”.
His father died when he was 16, and his mother moved back to England once he finished a college course to become a teacher.
He was deported in January after three failed attempts to remain in the country and is still fighting to return to Gothenburg, where he was hoping to build a family with his new wife.

blocks.caption: Caroline and John married recently in Sweden. Photograph: John Sellers

blocks.text: “Whenever I come to England, I feel like a tourist. Sweden is my home,” Sellers said.
“It is horrible. Not only do I feel like I’ve let down Caroline, I’ve let down my family, let down myself. I’ve been ripped from the love of my life, my other half.
“The pain is … I wish people wouldn’t have to go through this kind of pain, because you’re not whole. You’re broken.”
Hit with the cost of fighting deportation, and lack of work due to the deportation, he said he does not know how long it will be before he can physically hold his wife in his arms again.

Caroline, who has chronic conditions including fibromyalgia and symptoms of long Covid, including chronic fatigue, is trying to get back on her feet to return to teaching, but the case has caused a huge level of stress and upset.

She said: “It’s just horrible – the feeling of finally having someone to help you with things, someone to lean on and someone who is always there for you and then having to spend so much time, effort and money on fighting the government just to be able to continue that relationship.
“There are so many things we want to do. We just want to spend our lives together, and it’s so hard having to fight for that, especially when I am not well to begin with.”
Sweden’s migration minister, Johan Forssell, is poised to respond to Swedish MP Håkan Svenneling’s demand for a review of the approach to British residents in the country post-Brexit.
Svenneling intervened last month after it emerged one of his constituents, 78-year-old widow Joyce Thomas, who has been in the country for 21 years, was told to leave.

Thomas has until 7 September to leave, but her friends and supporters are pleading with Forssell to freeze removals and review a policy critics have said is not consistent with the Brexit withdrawal agreement.

Another elderly British citizen, George Mason, who is in full-time dementia care, was told to leave the country in August but has won a stay of execution until 28 September while the migration authorities consider the “obstacles to enforcement”, his son said.
The Guardian is aware of another British man detained by police on Tuesday and told he will be deported.
after newsletter promotion

Caroline Sellers said she and John decided to go to the media because it was important for politicians and officials in Brussels to see how Sweden’s interpretation of Brexit was “crushing people, crushing families” rather than protecting them, as politicians promised.

Eurostat data shows that Sweden has the highest number of Brexit-related deportations of Britons of all EU member states. About 2,500 British nationals have been ordered to leave the country since Brexit, one-third of the entire number of removal orders issued across the 27-member bloc since Brexit in 2021.

The problem centres on the Migration Agency’s apparent refusal to allow late applications from people who were not aware they had to formally apply to remain post-Brexit – a process used in only 12 other EU countries.
Before, Brexit deportation of an EU national to another member state was only permitted in exceptional circumstances involving threats to national security.
But in the post-Brexit scenario in Sweden, deportations of Britons have been ordered even when no crime is involved.

The UK Foreign Office has expressed concern on multiple occasions about Sweden’s approach to late applications. It is understood that senior officials at the European Commission are also watching with interest.
David Milstead, an activist with the Brits in Sweden group, wrote in the Guardian last month that complaints about the Swedish approach had first been made years ago.
Part of the problem, he says, stems from the lack of communication to registered British people living in the country, causing missed deadline applications.
He said the Sellers’ case was “yet another example of systemic failings in Sweden’s implementation of the withdrawal agreement”.

He added: “There are welcome signs that the Swedish government is taking these problems more seriously, although it is too early to know what will follow. Any remedial action needs to come soon, because people are suffering now.”

Sellers was aware that Brexit might affect his right to stay in the country and, without any communication from government authorities, he considered his best option was to apply for Swedish citizenship.
This he did in September 2021, before the Brexit deadline of 31 December that year.
Not only was his citizenship rejected, but two subsequent attempts to remain in the country under family rights in national migration laws via his partner, now his wife, were also turned down.

The latest adjudication, after he appealed against the first decision to refuse him residency on the grounds of a family relationship with Caroline, whom he had yet to marry, was that they had “not lived together abroad for an extended period of time”.
The migration court had noted that other evidence of a durable relationship was “insufficient”.
The Sellers are now appealing for a review of the judgment with fresh evidence.

articles.title: Ray Hadley used homophobic slur against Alan Jones after 2GB withdrew offer of $4m breakfast radio gig, court hears
articles.summary:
Hadley is giving evidence in trial of former 2GB rival Jones, 85, who has pleaded not guilty to 22 indecent assault and sexual touching charges

  • Get our

blocks.text: Broadcaster Ray Hadley has told a Sydney court he used a homophobic slur and derogatory names when talking about his colleague Alan Jones, after 2GB withdrew a secret offer of a $4m contract to take over Jones’s coveted breakfast slot.
Hadley agreed under cross-examination by defence barrister Gabrielle Bashir SC that he told police in 2019 that Jones had recruited colleagues at 2GB to “dig up some dirt” on him.
Jones is on trial over 20 charges of indecent assault and two counts of sexual touching involving six men. The 85-year-old has pleaded not guilty.
On his second day giving evidence at Downing Centre local court, Hadley testified that a colleague had told him Jones had “marshalled the troops and said ‘Dig up some dirt on Hadley’”.

Hadley in 2019 had walked into Jones’s office after being accused of an unrelated assault against a colleague, and called the breakfast host “a cunt and a dog”, according to a police statement from the time that was raised in court .
The assault allegation against Hadley was dropped when 2GB CCTV showed nothing had happened, Hadley told Jones’s trial.
Hadley agreed that he had “an animosity towards [Jones] at that time”. He said he often called him a “grub”, and that in a text exchange shown to him by Bashir he had called Jones “a faggot”.

Bashir, when defending Jones in court, has said the allegations against her client were “trial by media” fuelled by hatred and jealousy. Hadley “wanted to destroy” Jones and to “tear him apart”, the barrister has said previously.
Bashir put to Hadley on Wednesday that he was having a difficult time after his secret contract to replace Jones was torn up and Jones was re-signed in May 2019 for two more years.
“Not at all, I maintained the same job I’d done for the previous 17 years and inadvertently Mr Jones had doubled my salary,” Hadley replied.
after newsletter promotion
Hadley disagreed that the pinnacle of his career was attaining the breakfast radio slot, insisting that “going from $2m to $4m” while remaining on the Ray Hadley Morning Show was the pinnacle.
Hadley told the court he was approached by management in late 2018 and they said they’d had enough of Jones and his then-defamation cases and offered him the job.
“I didn’t want to get out of bed at 1.30am, but the money made me do it,” Hadley said.
Bashir suggested to Hadley that a later text to Jones – who was suffering from ill health – was rubbish. It read: “I love you.”
The trial before judge Glenn Walsh continues.

articles.title: Impeachment court chides prosec lawyer for ‘intramurals’, wasting time
articles.summary: MANILA, Philippines — Prosecution counsel Benjamin Tolosa Jr. received a scolding from the Senate impeachment court for engaging in “intramurals” with the defense lawyer and wasting time, after he…

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines — Prosecution counsel Benjamin Tolosa Jr. received a scolding from the Senate impeachment court for engaging in “intramurals” with the defense lawyer and wasting time, after he started his examination of former Education Undersecretary Michael Poa on Wednesday by asking if he is a competent lawyer.

At the resumption of Vice President Sara Duterte’s impeachment trial on Wednesday, Tolosa asked Poa — also a counsel for Duterte for these proceedings — regarding his educational background, his entry into the legal profession, and eventually being appointed into various positions in the Department of Education (DepEd).
When Tolosa asked whether Poa is a trusted official of Duterte, Sheila Sison, counsel for the respondent on duty, said she is willing to stipulate or agree to that matter.

But when Tolosa asked whether the defense would also stipulate that Poa is an “is an experienced and highly competent lawyer,” Sison fired back, asking if the prosecution is classifying Poa as an expert witness.
“Before I respond to that, may I now ask the prosecutor if they are qualifying this witness as an expert, your Honor,” Sison said.

“Because that is the inference from that proposal to stipulate, that he is highly experienced and of high expertise, in the work that he does, your Honor, as a lawyer. So earlier, they qualified him as a hostile witness and if they qualify him now as an expert, then that will give the prosecutor some leeway to ask him on legal matters,” she added.

Tolosa then said that the defense cannot dictate on the prosecution if they will consider Poa as an expert witness, as it falls under their discretion. However, Presiding Officer and Senator-judge Francis Escudero told Tolosa that he can just ask the questions as they are.

“With all due respect, the defense cannot dictate on the prosecution on the nature of the testimony of the witness. That discretion falls entirely and exclusively on us, if we want to present a witness as an expert witness, or ordinary witness. He may be the most qualified lawyer, but it’s still our discretion if we want to use him as an expert witness or not,” Tolosa said.

“Then in that case the chair will ask counsel to simply proceed with his questions because counsel, I find it irrelevant to be asking for a stipulation if Atty. Poa is good at what he does, I believe he is, but unless you will qualify him as an expert as pointed out by Atty. Sheila, instead of going through these intramurals,” Escudero replied.
Tolosa tried to interrupt, but Escudero firmly told him that the chair was making a ruling.
“Atty. Tolosa, Chair is ruling, kindly proceed with your direct examination already and go direct to your points,” Escudero said.

“But with all due respect, his competence is highly material to this case, because it will go into the credibility of his statements, and of course your Honor please, we be given some leeway because even if this is direct, because he is a hostile witness, this is the nature of our cross-examination,” Tolosa replied. “So we hope that we be allowed, we be given wider latitude in examining this witness.”

“Counsel, you are asking for a stipulation which the opposing counsel refused to do so again […] We’ve wasted enough time on these intramurals between you and counsel for respondent, just proceed with your direct. The witness is there, the witness is smart enough to answer,” Escudero added.

The atmosphere during Wednesday’s trial has been tense, as the impeachment court is presented with a unique situation, where a counsel for the respondent — in this case, Poa acting as Duterte’s lawyer — is asked by the prosecution to take the stand as a hostile witness.
Sison, lead counsel for Duterte, initially questioned Tolosa’s offer as he called Poa “abugadong walang alam” (lawyer who knows nothing) as it appears to be a mere “rhetoric aimed to provide drama.”

Tolosa said that it was not his intention to insult Poa, saying that he was merely referring to Poa’s insistence during a House of Representatives hearing in 2024 that he does not have personal knowledge of the confidential fund (CF) expenditures made by the DepEd for the first three quarters of 2023.
Still, Sison asked that the statements be stricken off the record, as Tolosa could have used better phrasing. Escudero agreed with Sison, ruling that Tolosa’s remarks be removed from the records.

Poa is the tenth witness presented by the prosecution for Article I of the Articles of Impeachment, which delves into allegations of CF misuse within Duterte’s offices — DepEd and the Office of the Vice President (OVP).

Before Tolosa, the prosecution panel presented two Land Bank of the Philippines officials from which OVP and DepEd withdrew their CFs; Commission on Audit (COA) auditors who checked on the confidential expenditures made by Duterte’s offices; OVP staffers like former special disbursing officer Gina Acosta; and on Tuesday, two Philippine Army (PA) officials.

During the trial on Tuesday, Army Col. Maranos Boransing II and Army Col. Magtanggol Panopio testified that none of Duterte’s offices — whether it be DepEd, OVP, or even the Vice Presidential Security and Protection Group — placed part of its regular allocations or CFs to their youth oriented-programs.

Boransing and Panopio were referring to the Youth Leadership Summit (YLS) and the Information Education Communication (IEC), programs funded by the PA’s annual budget, which aim to curb communist groups’ recruitment of high school and college students.

However, when the Commission on Audit (COA) flagged DepEd’s P15.54 million confidential expenditures through an audit observation memorandum (AOM), the department cited certifications from Boransing, Panopio and other PA officials regarding the conduct of the YLS and IEC to prove the use of CFs.
During the trial, Panopio also admitted being shocked that DepEd under Duterte used his certification to justify its confidential expenses. /gsg

articles.title: DepEd eyes higher budget to hire more school counselor associates
articles.summary: MANILA, Philippines — The Department of Education (DepEd) is set to request additional funding to hire more school counselor associates to address learners’ mental well-being. At the Kapihan sa…

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines — The Department of Education (DepEd) is set to request additional funding to hire more school counselor associates to address learners’ mental well-being.

At the Kapihan sa Manila Prince Hotel forum on Wednesday, DepEd Governance and Operations Undersecretary Malcolm Garma noted that the agency had already begun the process of hiring nearly 10,000 school counselor associates.
“Ipa-prioritize natin yung mga schools na, based on our mapping, yung hotspots where violence was recorded,” Garma explained.
(We will be prioritizing schools that, based on our mapping, are hotspots where violence was recorded.)
“[It’s] budget season, so we will be asking for more because that 10,000 [counselor associates] will not be enough for the more than 45,000 schools we have,” he added.
DepEd is scheduled to face the House of Representatives appropriations committee this coming Monday, September 7.
Garma noted that the department faced a challenge in hiring licensed guidance counselors.
In response to this challenge, according to the undersecretary, the agency hoped to “downgrade” some of the agency’s line items for registered guidance counselors to school counselor associates.
“Hindi ibig sabihin wala nang kakayahan itong associates to do counseling because they should be graduates of psychology or training in terms of behavioral science,” he explained.
(This does not mean, however, that associates have no capability to do counseling because they should be graduates of psychology or have training in terms of behavioral science.)
“We are optimistic that the hiring of counselor associates would be a game-changer in many schools,” he added.

There are only around 5,000 registered guidance counselors in the Philippines, with only 1,000 serving under DepEd, the agency’s human resource and organizational development Undersecretary Willie Cabral said in August.
Guidance counseling in schools regained public attention following the fatal school shootings in Tacloban City last June 22 and Zamboanga City last August 18.

Although psychologists have reportedly also attributed the perpetrators’ actions to other factors apart from their state of mind, the incidents renewed interest in child and adolescent mental health. /jpv

articles.title: DOH warns of compromised programs due to possible 2027 budget cut
articles.summary: MANILA, Philippines — Some programs of the Department of Health (DOH) may be compromised due to the budget cuts the agency is facing in the 2027 National Expenditure Program (NEP) over its original…

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines — Some programs of the Department of Health (DOH) may be compromised due to the budget cuts the agency is facing in the 2027 National Expenditure Program (NEP) over its original proposed budget, Health Secretary Edwin Mercado said on Wednesday.

During the House committee on appropriations’ briefing on the DOH’s proposed budget for 2027, Mercado shared that the DOH and its attached agencies originally proposed P837 billion, which is significantly bigger than the P353.8 billion budget allocated for the agency under the NEP.
In his presentation, Mercado said that the proposed budget under the NEP is allocated among five pillars:

items: Pillar 1: healthy schools, workplaces, and communities (P60.5 billion)
Pillar 2: functional primary care system (P29.1 billion)
Pillar 3: quality and efficient hospitals (207.3 billion)
Pillar 4: Information technology transformation
Pillar 5: strong institutions and health workforce (P54.2 billion)

blocks.text: Mercado also noted that of the proposed budget in the NEP, maintenance and other operating expenses comprised a huge chunk of the funding (P218 billion), followed by personnel services (P112 billion), and capital outlay (P19 billion).
Rep. Dadah Ismula then asked Mercado about the programs that would suffer the most if they did not restore the department’s original budget proposal.
Mercado said one of the programs is the Health Facilities Enhancement Program (HFEP), with a proposed budget of P29 billion which was slashed to P14 billion under the NEP.
The HFEP enables government health facilities to provide quality healthcare through allocation of capital outlays for improvement of infrastructures and equipment.
He added that the DOH’s hospital operations suffered an P11 billion budget cut.
He also shared that the Philippine Health Insurance Corporation suffered budget cuts as it originally proposed P379 billion but only got P73 billion under the NEP.
“Yun yung top 3 na medyo hindi naibigay yung aming narequest,” Mercado said.
(That’s the top three programs that did not get what we requested.)
Ismula said funding for the health care of Filipinos should not be depleted as many healthcare assistance programs will be compromised.

“Hindi pwedeng tapyasan ang budget ng healthcare. Lalo ngayon, tumataas ang cases ng leptospirosis, dengue kada baha at bumabata ang nagkakacancer o kinakailangang i-dialysis dahil sa kidney disease,” Ismula said.

articles.title: Power supply alerts raised in Occidental Mindoro
articles.summary: The Occidental Mindoro Electric Cooperative (OMECO) warned consumers to brace for possible power supply disruptions on Wednesday as several generating units of the Occidental Mindoro Consolidated…

blocks.text: The Occidental Mindoro Electric Cooperative (OMECO) warned consumers to brace for possible power supply disruptions on Wednesday as several generating units of the Occidental Mindoro Consolidated Power Corp. (OMCPC) undergo corrective maintenance.

CALAPAN CITY — The Occidental Mindoro Electric Cooperative (OMECO) warned consumers to brace for possible power supply disruptions on Wednesday as several generating units of the Occidental Mindoro Consolidated Power Corp. (OMCPC) undergo corrective maintenance.
OMECO said it placed the mainland Occidental Mindoro power system under red alert from 1 p.m. to 2 p.m. and yellow alert from 10 a.m. to noon, 3 p.m. to 4 p.m., and 7 p.m. to 8 p.m.
The alerts were attributed to limited available generating capacity from OMCPC power plants.
OMECO said the Sablayan Diesel Power Plant, which has a contracted capacity of 6 megawatts, currently had only 4 MW of dependable capacity, with Units 1 and 4 undergoing corrective maintenance.
At the Pulang Lupa Diesel Power Plant, which has 5.8 MW of dependable capacity, Unit 5 was also under corrective maintenance.
Meanwhile, the OMCPC MAPSA Plant, with a contracted capacity of 9 MW, had only 5.4 MW of dependable capacity available as Units 6, 7, 9 and 11 were undergoing corrective maintenance.
OMECO said the reduced generating capacity could affect electricity supply in some areas, depending on the power system’s actual condition./coa

articles.title: This is not standard flooding; it is Himalayan tsunami – Nepal minister
articles.summary: KATHMANDU — Following the unprecedented disaster in Rasuwa and surrounding northern districts, Nepal finds itself in the grip of a profound humanitarian and infrastructural crisis. Foreign…

blocks.text: KATHMANDU — Following the unprecedented disaster in Rasuwa and surrounding northern districts, Nepal finds itself in the grip of a profound humanitarian and infrastructural crisis. Foreign Affairs Minister Shisir Khanal speaks about the scale of the disaster, the logistical nightmare of high-altitude tunnel rescues, and why Nepal is shifting its diplomatic posture from requesting humanitarian aid to demanding climate compensation.
This Q&A has been edited for clarity and length, and is based on an interview on Kantipur TV’s Fireside by Rupesh Shrestha.
Minister, you recently returned from a field visit to Nuwakot. What is the real-world scale of this disaster?

When the first reports came in around 9am, our immediate conceptual imagery of a “flood” was a standard seasonal rise in river levels. But having spent the day in Nuwakot, I realized how limited our vocabulary is.

This was not a standard flood. With wave heights reaching 20 to 30 meters and speeds clocked at 180 kilometers per hour, this was a disaster of tornado-like velocity—what many are rightly calling a “Himalayan Tsunami”. It is a scale of disaster that is entirely outside the living memory of Nepal.

The damage is immense. Early assessments indicate that ten municipalities across Nuwakot, Rasuwa, and Dhading—spanning 30 to 32 wards—have been heavily impacted, with additional damage downstream in Gorkha and Chitwan. We are looking at tens of thousands of damaged private homes, alongside heavily hit schools and multi-billion-rupee hydropower projects.
There has been criticism that the government was slow to seek international help, choosing instead to rely on its own resources. How do you respond to this?

There was absolutely no delay or rigidity on our part. The disaster unfolded rapidly. By 11am, while the floodwaters were still surging toward Dhading, the prime minister convened the National Disaster Council and mobilized security forces for immediate search and rescue.

Our initial priority was saving lives on the surface. By the second day, as our ground teams assessed the buried hydropower projects, they reported a critical need for highly specialized tunnel rescue support. We communicated this need immediately.

Because of high-altitude weather and transport limitations, airlift was the only viable option. Despite heavy cloud cover on the third afternoon that delayed flights, the Indian specialized tunnel rescue team arrived on the ground by the evening of the third day. The Chinese specialized team arrived by the afternoon of the fourth day, and a South Korean team is actively working at the Upper Trishuli site. Within 72 hours of identifying the need, international specialized rescue operations were fully operational on-site.
What is the status of the rescue operations at the buried hydropower tunnels, such as Trishuli 3A and Chilime? Is there still hope of finding survivors?

We must maintain hope and exhaust every possibility. Historically, there are global precedents—such as the 2018 Thailand cave rescue, or tunnel incidents in India in 2023 and China in 2021—where survivors were rescued after 14 to 18 days due to natural air pockets. Even if a tunnel is partially blocked, if there are air pockets, survival is possible.

However, the public must understand the extreme complexity on the ground. This is a highly complex disaster. These are not simple horizontal cave openings. The entire topography has shifted; hillsides have sheared off, leaving vertical cliffs covered in deep, unstable debris. In some areas, our rescue teams are literally sinking into quicksand-like mud.

At Trishuli 3A, teams had to locate the buried tunnel entrance using engineered maps because the surface construction was entirely erased. Instead of drilling horizontally, rescuers had to dig a vertical shaft—like a 30-foot well—just to reach the concrete crown of the tunnel. Once they breached it, they immediately began pumping in oxygen.

Currently, the Chinese team is working at the Trishuli 3A site, the Indian teams are deployed at Chilime and Langtang, and the South Korean team is coordinating at Upper Trishuli. While our security forces successfully cleared and entered the final points of the Rasuwagadhi tunnel on Monday, unfortunately, no survivors or bodies were recovered there. We are continuing to mobilise every local and international resource available.

The Rasuwagadhi-Kerung border is closed, and there are reports of temporary closures at Tatopani. How is the government managing bilateral trade and stranded travellers, particularly Mansarovar pilgrims?

Our northern supply chains and tourist corridors have been severely disrupted. Because the Tibet Autonomous Region is highly sensitive, Chinese regulations typically dictate that travelers must exit through the exact border post they entered.

To bypass this restriction, we actively negotiated with Chinese authorities to allow stranded Nepalis and foreign tourists to exit via alternative crossings. Stranded Nepalis have already begun returning through the Hilsa crossing in Humla. Furthermore, we have formally requested that the Korola border crossing in Mustang be used to evacuate foreign tourists who cannot return via Rasuwagadhi.

Regarding trade, hundreds of cargo trucks are currently stranded on the Chinese side of the Rasuwagadhi border. We have requested permission from Chinese authorities to reroute these cargo flows through the Tatopani and Korola crossings to prevent a total collapse of our northern supply lines.
You have stated that Nepal will no longer treat post-disaster assistance as mere “humanitarian aid” or bilateral grants. What is the government’s new diplomatic strategy?

Nepal’s greenhouse gas emissions are virtually negligible. Yet, we are paying the ultimate price for a global crisis we did not create. The rapid melting of glaciers and these catastrophic mountain tsunamis are direct consequences of global climate change.

We are shifting our diplomatic framework from “aid” to “justice and compensation”. This is not a matter of charity; it is a matter of legal and moral liability. The major industrial emitters—such as China, which is the world’s top emitter, the United States at number two, and India at number three—have a historical responsibility to compensate vulnerable nations like Nepal.

To this end, the Ministry of Finance has officially dispatched a formal climate compensation claim letter to our international partners. We will be raising this issue with absolute firmness and clarity at every upcoming international forum. This is a matter of civilizational survival. If our Himalayan glaciers disappear, the water security of over two billion people in South Asia—dependent on rivers like the Ganges and the Trishuli—will be permanently compromised. We are advocating not just for Nepal, but for the survival of South Asian civilization.

There is a strong perception that the government is more active on social media than on the ground, and that citizen deaths are treated merely as statistics. Why does Prime Minister Balendra Shah use his personal Facebook page to disseminate official government updates instead of official institutional channels? What about citizens who are not on social media, or cannot read?

For those whose family members are still missing or out of contact, their grief and frustration are completely understandable, and the government’s sole objective is to mobilize every available resource to find them. A citizen’s life is never just a number to us; it represents a family’s entire future, hope, and happiness.

Regarding the prime minister’s communications, his personal Facebook page has been his primary political platform since the very beginning of his public career. It has millions of followers, making it mathematically the most immediate and effective channel to reach a massive audience. While the Prime Minister’s Office maintains its own official communication handles, the reach on his personal page is far greater. These updates are immediately picked up by mainstream newspapers, television networks, and radio stations. This broadcast ensures that regular video and audio reports are generated, effectively reaching citizens who are not on social media or are illiterate.

Many citizens stranded in temporary camps, such as Laharepauwa, complain that while they see helicopters flying overhead, actual relief supplies—food, clothing, and sanitary products—are not reaching them. How is the government regulating relief distribution?

We recognize these grievances and are working to streamline the supply chain. In the initial rescue phase, helicopter flights are centralized and highly fluid—sometimes flying to extract a single stranded individual, which is highly inefficient from a resource perspective but necessary to save lives.

For the relief phase, we have established a strict coordination mechanism. Relief materials are dispatched only after direct coordination with local Ward Presidents to ensure they go where they are actually needed.

Regarding financial transparency, the Prime Minister’s Disaster Relief Fund has already received over Rs5 billion in public and diaspora contributions. This fund is heavily regulated and will be strictly channelled into immediate relief operations and long-term reconstruction. We are fully committed to ensuring that not a single rupee of these public donations is wasted on unnecessary administrative overheads or government luxury travel. We will stand firmly with our citizens through the rescue, relief, and eventual reconstruction phases. /dl

articles.title: Panaon seascape marks first year with management plan
articles.summary: MANILA, Philippines — The Panaon Island Protected Seascape (PIPS) in Southern Leyte has completed its first year as a protected area, with its management board established and a plan approved to…

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines — The Panaon Island Protected Seascape (PIPS) in Southern Leyte has completed its first year as a protected area, with its management board established and a plan approved to guide the protection of its marine ecosystems, conservationists said.

The milestone came as Oceana, local governments and communities marked the first anniversary of Republic Act No. 12238, which placed roughly 60,000 hectares of waters around Panaon Island under protected status.
The law, signed on Aug. 29, 2025, covers the municipalities of Liloan, San Francisco, Pintuyan and San Ricardo.

blocks.caption: Graphics by Ed Lustan/Inquirer.net

blocks.text: Oceana said the Protected Area Management Board (PAMB) has been established and its executive committee has approved the Protected Area Management Plan (PAMP), which will serve as a guide for coordinated enforcement, protection of marine ecosystems and sustainable tourism in the seascape.

The PAMP was developed with the Southern Leyte State University-Bontoc Campus, the Department of Environment and Natural Resources (DENR), the four municipal governments, the provincial government of Southern Leyte, local communities and other stakeholders.

“One year down, a lifetime to go! The Panaon Island Protected Seascape law is coming to life, through the incredible teamwork of local governments, national agencies and stakeholders. Their passion and stewardship are the tide that will lift our fisheries, biodiversity and the coastal livelihoods for generations,” Oceana Vice President Von Hernandez said.
Marine life, livelihoods
Panaon Island is part of the Coral Triangle and is among the world’s 50 priority reefs identified as likely to withstand the impacts of climate change, according to Oceana.
A 2019 reef assessment found that parts of the island had up to 60 percent very good coral cover, compared with a national average of 20 percent.
The area is also home to whale sharks, locally known as tiki-tiki, as well as green and hawksbill sea turtles. A rare and endangered blue whale has also been sighted within the seascape.

blocks.caption: Graphics by Ed Lustan/Inquirer.net

blocks.text: Pintuyan, one of the municipalities covered by PIPS, is known for whale shark interactions.
Pintuyan Mayor Ricarte Estrella said protecting the marine ecosystem could also help sustain the municipality’s tourism and other community livelihoods.

“As Pintuyan is known for its whale shark interactions, the implementation of Panaon Island as a protected seascape has helped protect and maintain our marine ecosystem. A healthier ecosystem supports more plankton, which is the primary food source of whale sharks,” Estrella said.
“When the marine environment thrives, whale sharks are more likely to stay in our municipal waters, which in turn supports our community livelihoods,” he added.

blocks.caption: Graphics by Ed Lustan/Inquirer.net

blocks.text: Fisherfolk have also supported community-managed marine protected areas and fishery reserves in Panaon, helping lay the groundwork for the protected seascape, Oceana said.
The DENR is set to establish a Protected Area Management Office (PAMO) on the island to oversee the day-to-day management of PIPS.

Meanwhile, the Department of Science and Technology (DOST) and the Bureau of Fisheries and Aquatic Resources (BFAR), through its Fisheries and Coastal Resiliency Project, have begun supporting sustainable livelihood and coastal resource management initiatives.
Possible support from the Department of Trade and Industry and the Department of Labor and Employment is being explored, according to Oceana.
Speed limits for boats

A landmark provision in Republic Act No. 12238 provides for speed limits for vessels passing through PIPS waters to help protect whale sharks and other large marine animals from injury and disturbance, particularly in areas used for feeding and migration.
Section 8 of the law directs the DENR, Philippine Coast Guard and other enforcement agencies to adopt appropriate speed regulations.
Hernandez said the first year of implementation showed the importance of cooperation among government agencies and communities.

“The implementation of the Panaon Seascape plan is a testament to what happens when national agencies, local leaders and island communities paddle in the same direction to turn our vision of a living, breathing sanctuary into reality. Together, we are building a legacy of abundance and coastal resilience,” he said. /dm

articles.title: Jailed HK activist Joshua Wong pleads guilty to foreign collusion
articles.summary: Wong, 29, is already in prison on subversion charges under the controversial National Security Law.

blocks.text: Prominent Hong Kong pro-democracy campaigner Joshua Wong has pleaded guilty to collusion with foreign entities, a charge that carries a maximum sentence of life in prison under Beijing's sweeping National Security Law (NSL).

The 29-year-old, who has become the poster child for political activism in Hong Kong, is already serving a sentence of four years and eight months after being convicted of subversion – another NSL violation – in late 2024.
The court said Wong would be sentenced at a later date. His earlier jail term is due to end early next year.
Wong was at the forefront of the Umbrella Movement in 2014 and massive pro-democracy protests in 2019.

The latest charge accuses Wong of conspiring with other campaigners, including exiled activist Nathan Law, to ask foreign countries and entities outside China to impose sanctions or blockades against Beijing.

These include activities that took place between July and late November 2020, the court heard. That was the year China introduced the controversial NSL, which critics say has created a climate of fear and quashed dissent in Hong Kong.
Beijing and Hong Kong authorities argue the law is necessary to maintain stability and deny it has weakened autonomy.
On Tuesday, the court heard that Wong and Law had participated in "international lobbying on numerous occasions", including via visits to the US, Germany and Italy.
The duo are among several leaders who founded the pro-democracy party Demosistō in April 2016, and ran for the Hong Kong Legislative Council elections that year.

Among other things, prosecutors on Tuesday also accused Wong, along with Law, of promoting the Hong Kong Human Rights and Democracy Act: a US federal law that came into force in November 2019, during Donald Trump's first administration. The Act compels the US government to impose sanctions against mainland China and Hong Kong officials if they are deemed responsible for human rights abuses in Hong Kong.
Even after Demosistō disbanded, Wong had maintained that he would not abandon his political stance and would continue to seek support from the international community, the prosecutors said.
Wong, dressed in a dark blue shirt and dark-rimmed glasses, did not dispute these allegations.
About 40 of Wong's supporters, including fellow activists and some of his close friends, gathered in court on Tuesday. Some shouted: "Hang in there, Joshua!"
Wong was seen smiling and nodding in response from the dock.

Tsang Kin-shing, a former member of the now-dissolved League of Social Democrats, said he hopes the court will impose a lenient sentence, noting that Wong has by now spent more than 2,000 days in prison.
Fellow activist Louis Lee said Wong and his supporters were disheartened that he was handed another NSL charge while already serving time in prison.
Wong has continued seeking out new interests while in prison, including learning how to play the guitar and working out.
"I hope everyone can learn from him," Lee says.

articles.title: Marcos: National gov't to provide P300M for bridge repair in Tarlac City
articles.summary: The national government will provide P300 million for bridge repair in Tarlac City following the impact of the southwest monsoon or Habagat, President Ferdinand "Bongbong" Marcos Jr. said Wednesday.

blocks.text: Published September 2, 2026 12:24pm
The national government will provide P300 million for bridge repair in Tarlac City following the impact of the southwest monsoon or Habagat, President Ferdinand "Bongbong" Marcos Jr. said Wednesday.
Marcos made the announcement during an inspection of the damaged Agana Bridge and Aquino Bridge.
"Para maging mas mabilis ang trabaho, we will be downloading P300 million to the local government dahil ito ay local bridge. Kaya sila kailangan ang magtatrabaho dito," Marcos said.
(To make the job faster, we will be downloading P300 million to the local government because it is a local bridge. They will be the ones who will do the work here.)
"Siyempre, tutulungan natin sa technical aspects. We will help them in every way that we can," he added.
(Of course, we will help them in the technical aspects. We will help them in every way that we can.)
A Bailey bridge—made of steel panels and pins for rapid construction—is now being assembled to temporarily replace the section of Agana Bridge that was washed away.
Marcos said the temporary bridge is expected to allow pedestrian traffic within a week, while light vehicles could be allowed to cross within two weeks.
Initially, vans and other vehicles weighing 10 tons or less may be allowed to use the bridge.
For Aquino Bridge, Marcos said repairs may take longer because of the extent of the damage.
He said the damage of the two bridges has left Gerona as the only remaining alternative route for the affected areas.
Marcos described the flooding as unprecedented and attributed the extreme rainfall and flooding to the effects of climate change. — VDV, GMA News

articles.title: Hong Kong pro-democracy activist Joshua Wong pleads guilty in second national security case
articles.summary:
Wong, 29, is accused of urging foreign powers to impose sanctions, blockades and other hostile measures against China

Joshua…

blocks.text: Joshua Wong, one of Hong Kong’s most prominent pro-democracy activists, pleaded guilty on Wednesday to conspiring to seek foreign sanctions against Hong Kong and China, a national security charge that carries a maximum life sentence.
Prosecutors have accused Wong, 29, of working with the exiled Hong Kong activist Nathan Law to urge foreign powers to impose sanctions, blockades or other hostile measures against China.
The court heard that Wong had visited foreign countries and met foreign politicians to lobby for sanctions against Hong Kong and China.
The prosecution said he had continued to call for sanctions on Hong Kong and China after the implementation of the national security law and that he had posted meetings on his social media accounts.
Wong has been continuously imprisoned since November 2020. He has spent nearly six years in detention and had been due to be released in January 2027.
In 2022 he pleaded guilty to conspiracy to commit subversion for his role in an unofficial primary election. In November 2024 he was sentenced to four years and eight months in prison.
Wong waved at supporters as he entered the dock. He wore a blue shirt and black-rimmed glasses. He stood with his arms behind his back as he pleaded guilty to the charges.

Wong is expected to be sentenced later. The offence is punishable by a prison term of three to 10 years, or up to life imprisonment if the offence is deemed to be “of a grave nature”. Pleading guilty could typically result in a reduced sentence.
Outside Hong Kong’s high court, people queued overnight to secure a seat at Wednesday’s hearing.

blocks.caption: Hong Kong activist and supporters hold signs during a press event to support pro-democracy activist Joshua Wong in Taipei, Taiwan, on Wednesday. Photograph: Chiang Ying-ying/AP

blocks.text: In 2014, the then teenage Wong became the international face of the Umbrella Movement, when thousands of protesters occupied major roads across Hong Kong for 79 days demanding greater democracy. In October 2014 he appeared on the cover of a Time magazine under the headline: “The Face of Protest”.

When protests erupted in 2019 over a proposed extradition bill, Wong was serving a prison sentence for his role in the 2014 demonstrations. He was released at the height of the movement and immediately joined calls for the bill to be withdrawn.

In 2020 Beijing imposed a wide-ranging national security law on Hong Kong after a year of anti-government protests. The authorities said the law was needed to restore stability to the international financial hub. Critics say six years on the law is continuing to expand in scope.

Wong is the only activist in Hong Kong prosecuted twice under the law. Supporters say the prosecution heavily relied on his advocacy before the national security law was enacted and argue his case has been applied retroactively.

“It’s obvious that the government wants to keep him behind bars for as long as they can, so as to isolate him and not to let him become a visible symbol of resistance.” said Frances Hui from the Committee for Freedom in Hong Kong Foundation.
Wong’s case has attracted widespread condemnation from global rights organisations.

“By stacking one charge after another against Joshua Wong, the authorities are ensuring that the democracy icon stays behind bars, silencing him and the Hong Kong pro-democracy movement he helped lead and inspire,” said Elaine Pearson, Asia director at Human Rights Watch.

“Conflating promoting democracy and free speech with undermining national security is a favourite dodge for authoritarians. Beijing also likes blaming ‘hostile’, but unspecified foreign forces,” said Sophie Richardson, a longtime China rights advocate.
On Tuesday the former Conservative leader Iain Duncan Smith urged the UK government to raise Wong’s case with Beijing, saying: “Enough is enough. It’s time to stop chasing peaceful protesters.”
With Associated Press

articles.title: Zelensky says airlines should avoid Russian airspace as Ukraine escalates drone operations
articles.summary: Chinese and Gulf state airlines are among those still using Russian airspace. Meanwhile, Russia says it will intensify its own attacks on Ukraine.

blocks.text: Ukraine's president has told airlines that Russian airspace will be "effectively closing" as his country escalates its drone strikes.
"We want to warn every airline that uses Russian airspace, every insurer, everyone who still uses key Russian airports: the Russian sky is becoming completely dangerous," Volodymyr Zelensky says.
Most Western commercial airlines do not fly over Russia as a consequence of the ongoing Russian invasion of Ukraine, but carriers in countries such as China do.

Russian President Vladimir Putin responded by saying that Zelensky's comments amounted to a "declaration of state terrorism", while adding that Russia would continue its own intensifying attacks on Ukraine.
Explaining the elevated airspace risk, Zelensky said: "Ukraine does not threaten civilian aviation as such - not a single civilian aircraft.
"There will simply be drones in Russia's skies on a scale that has to be taken into account," he said in his nightly video address on Tuesday.
Zelensky said that "the war started by Russia is closing its skies".
He directed the warning to airlines continuing to operate flights to Russian airports, especially in major cities like St Petersburg and Moscow.
Ukraine has targeted energy facilities deep inside Russian territory in addition to large retailers.

Aviation risk advisory firm Osprey Flight Solutions said in an alert to clients that while the majority of Ukraine's drone and missile strikes were likely to occur within 300km (186 miles) of the border, daily attacks deeper inside Russia were almost certain to continue this year.

"There is also a realistic possibility that the frequency of Ukrainian strikes will continue to increase in the short term deep inside Russian territory," the alert added. "It is assessed that miscalculation and/or misidentification is likely in areas related to the Ukraine conflict."
Speaking to reporters at the Shanghai Co-operation Organisation summit in Kyrgyzstan, Putin said: "They are asking us to resume negotiations... but you don't negotiate with terrorists."

His comments come as Russia's attacks on Ukraine continue, with heavy strikes killing 12 people on Monday. The military has said it is preparing to carry out "massive" strikes on Ukrainian power stations.
Putin also acknowledged that Ukrainian strikes had damaged infrastructure inside Russia, while insisting that "only 10%" of oil refineries were left to repair.
Chinese, Turkish and Gulf state airlines are among those using Russian airspace, with savings in time and fuel on routes between Asia and Europe.
Other carriers have largely avoided the eastern European region since the beginning of Russia's full-scale invasion in February, 2022.
Ukraine has closed its airspace to civilian aircraft since the beginning of the war.
Last year, the UN aviation agency ruled that Russia was responsible for the downing of Malaysia Airlines Flight MH17 over eastern Ukraine in July 2014.
All 298 people on board the passenger plane were killed when it was shot down by a Russian-made missile. The Kremlin has always denied any responsibility for the air disaster.
In 2024, Putin apologised to the president of neighbouring Azerbaijan over the downing of a commercial airliner in Russian airspace, in which 38 people were killed.
He said the "tragic incident" had occurred when Russian air defence systems were repelling Ukrainian drones.

articles.title: PNP steps up police presence as '-ber' months begin
articles.summary: The Philippine National Police (PNP) on Wednesday said it has stepped up police visibility and patrols in areas expected to draw larger crowds as the country enters the “-ber” months, referring to…

blocks.text: Published September 2, 2026 12:22pm

As the "-ber" months usher in the Yuletide season on Tuesday, September 1, 2026, vendors in Divisoria, Binondo, Manila, prepare Christmas trees and other decorations for sale at the lowest prices. The Philippines is known for having the longest Christmas celebration. DANNY PATA

The Philippine National Police (PNP) on Wednesday said it has stepped up police visibility and patrols in areas expected to draw larger crowds as the country enters the “-ber” months, referring to September through December, which many Filipinos consider the start of the Christmas season.

PNP chief Police General Jose Melencio Nartatez Jr. directed regional and city police offices to strengthen patrols and monitoring in commercial establishments, transport terminals, markets and other public places.

“We have directed our police units to strengthen police visibility, patrols and monitoring in areas where people are expected to converge, particularly commercial establishments, transport terminals, markets, and other public places,” Nartatez said in a statement.
“Our priority is to prevent crimes before they happen and ensure a safe and peaceful holiday season,” he added.
Nartatez urged the public to remain vigilant against theft, robbery, scams and other crimes that could take advantage of increased consumer activity, cash transactions and travel.
He also reminded the public to secure their belongings, avoid sharing their real-time locations online and immediately report suspicious activities to the police.
The PNP said patrols would also be strengthened in crime-prone areas and communities where holiday activities are expected to increase.
Police units were also directed to coordinate closely with local authorities and other stakeholders to address emerging security concerns.— MCG, GMA News
