Airlink, a sponsor of the South African rugby union team, said that the flyby was conducted according to safety regulations. The airline said that it was carefully planned and rehearsed, with the aircraft travelling at around 150 knots (172 mph), when they went over the stadium. Each jet had three senior captains on board, Airlink said, operating in the roles of a commander, a co-pilot and a safety officer. The jets were not carrying any passengers.

“Airlink notes the concerns expressed in various social media and online forums regarding yesterday’s formation flyby over Cape Town’s DHL Stadium,” Airlink said on Sunday. “The flight demanded careful planning and rehearsal, as it required navigating at low altitude, at around 150 knots. The South African Civil Aviation Authority and Air Traffic Navigation Services provided valuable guidance, approval and support to ensure a safe flyby.”

blocks.caption: The planes fly above the stadium before kick-off. Photograph: Gallo Images/Getty Images

blocks.text: South African rugby union has a tradition of stadium flybys at big games, starting when a Boeing 747 flew over another stadium in Johannesburg before the 1995 World Cup final between the same teams, who are fierce rivals. But this weekend’s flyby was especially low and dramatic, generating global interest after it was shown as part of the pre-game broadcast, and sparking a flurry of videos shot by witnesses.

blocks.caption: The second jet flies through a cloud of pink dust that shot up from the stadium roof as part of the show. Photograph: AP

blocks.text: Some aviation experts questioned whether the margin for error was too small. “Basically, that lead aircraft … was kind of like dodging over the roof and climbing over the one side and dipping below and then climbing over the other side. That was a little bit uncomfortable,” said Chris Martinus, president of Aircraft Owners and Pilots Association South Africa. “[If] something adverse happens, you just don’t have options at that kind of altitude.”
after newsletter promotion

Keith Tonkin, an Australian aviation consultant and former military and commercial pilot, said on Monday that the Embraer passenger jets – which are small-to-medium jets designed for regional flights – were not designed or intended for that kind of low-level operation and warned against the precedent.

“The bigger picture is that a benchmark has been established and others may expect to do something similar, and that’s not going to end well,” Tonkin said. He added that turbulence or a bird strike at such a low altitude could leave the pilots with too little room to manoeuvre without hitting the stadium.
Airlink said that the flight data recorded by both aircraft confirmed that their flights were performed within civil aviation safety limits for speed and altitude.

articles.title: Canada's Carney holds firm against Trump tariffs
articles.summary: Canada is facing new US import penalties after Prime Minister Mark Carney refused to match US tariffs on China. Other countries are watching as the Trump trade clash turns into a fight over economic…

image.caption: Carney refuses to subordinate Canada’s trade policy to WashingtonImage: Jacques Boissinot/ZUMA/IMAGO

blocks.text: Canada has been quietly praised for refusing to fold under pressure from US President Donald Trump in the long-running fight over trade tariffs.
The latest talks between the North American neighbors collapsed on August 21. Until the 11th hour, both sides were talking as if a deal was within reach.
The United States then put 50% tariffs on about $20 billion (€17.2 billion) worth of Canadian goods, while Ottawa pledged to match those duties on US imports.
Until the talks folded, Canada's approach was to cut a deal that would reduce the tariffs and keep cross-border supply chains functioning, particularly in the automotive and steel sectors.
US negotiators were, however, accused of changing the terms at the last minute, which the Canadian side said would have forced them to match US tariffs on China.
According to Ottawa, Washington wanted a say on future trade deals with other nations and to prevent Chinese goods being routed through Canada to evade US duties.
Trade spat becomes sovereignty issue

Dan Ciuriak, a senior fellow at the Waterloo, Canada-based Center for International Governance Innovation, described Trump's tariff-matching plan as "fortress North America," which he said was now a sovereignty issue for Ottawa.
"Canada is a trading nation," Ciuriak told DW. "If we align perfectly with the Americans — primarily about China — we then end up sacrificing our trade policy."

There is a recent precedent. When the US imposed 100% tariffs on Chinese electric vehicles last year, Canada followed suit. Beijing retaliated with 100% tariffs against one of Canada's biggest exports — canola.
Canada's $4.9 billion exports of canola oil, meal and seed to China were cut in half last year, according to data from the Canada China Business Council.
Why Canada rejected Trump's terms despite economic risks
"The smaller country is the one that bears the brunt in this kind of game. So that's one very good reason for Canada to have an independent trade policy," said Ciuriak.

As the US-Canada talks collapsed, Ottawa also complained that Washington had sought relief from rules on French-language movies and shows. Canada said this amounted to interference in its language and culture.
Canadians back walk away from US
Despite the uncertainty and higher cost to business from walking away, the Canadian prime minister's approach to negotiations with the US has broad public support.
A survey conducted by the Angus Reid Institute found that three-in-four Canadians backed the more hard-line move, despite concerns over the impact on the domestic economy.
Ciuriak noted how Trump's barbs of turning Canada into the 51st US state and threats to rename Lake Ontario to Lake America have emboldened ordinary Canadians to boycott US travel and products.
"Travel by Canadians to the United States has plummeted," he said. "There has been a popular consumer backlash against buying American products."
New government data show Canadians made nearly 500,000 fewer trips to the US in the first three months of 2026 and spent about $800 million less on those visits.
A survey last month by the Angus Reid Institute found that 40% of Canadian grocery shoppers were checking product origins, and that most of those shoppers avoided US goods when they could.

blocks.caption: Trump has ordered US officials to rename Lake Ontario to 'Lake America'Image: Al Drago/UPI Photo/IMAGO

blocks.text: Although the two economies are tightly bound together, the new US duties apply to only about 5% of the $382 billion in goods that Canada exports to its southern neighbor.

The Royal Bank of Canada has warned that a no-deal would impact 0.4% of gross domestic product (GDP) and jobs, while University of Calgary economist Trevor Tombe estimated it could cost as many as 90,000 jobs.
Canada's stance closely watched globally
Other governments are also watching to see how standing up to Trump plays out.

During their own negotiations, the European Union, United Kingdom, Japan, South Korea and dozens of smaller partners all agreed to lower tariffs in return for market access, investment pledges or alignment with US policy.
Only China has so far met Trump's tariff threat head-on, matching tariffs with tariffs and negotiating as a fellow superpower, rather than taking the first deal on offer.
Speaking at the World Economic Forum in Davos in January, Carney said middle powers must act together, warning that if they were "not at the table," they would be "on the menu."

blocks.caption: Trump has threatened higher tariffs on Canadian automakers from JanuaryImage: Dax Melmer/The Canadian Press/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: But for now, Carney is holding the line largely on his own. New Canadian tariffs on $20 billion worth of US goods — including steel, aluminum, dairy, electronics and farm equipment — take effect on September 8. They are likely to be met with US retaliation.
While matching US tariffs dollar-for-dollar sounds aggressive, Ciuriak thinks they need not "punish" the Canadian economy.

"Canada's tariffs ... apply to products Canada both buys from and sells to the US. As American tariffs cut off Canadian sales south of the border, the Canadian measures create space at home for that production."
New Trump pressure on Canadian autos
From January, Trump has threatened to raise duties on Canadian autos, trucks, parts and steel unless production moves to the US.

He also refused to extend the United States–Mexico–Canada Agreement (USMCA) for another 16 years. Instead, the North American free-trade pact, which still covers most cross-border goods, will be reviewed year by year.
Will Canada cancel its order for US-made F-35 jets?

With no new talks planned with the US, Canadian lawmakers are talking up trade opportunities in other markets and weighing other retaliatory measures, including backing away from an order for US fighter jets.
Canada had planned to buy 88 Lockheed Martin F-35s, with 16 already on order. The rest are now on hold.
"When your friend kicks you in the back, one of the first rules is you don't then go and buy $12 billion of fighter jets from that person," British Columbia Premier David Eby said last week.

articles.title: Saxony-Anhalt State Premier Schulze takes on far-right AfD
articles.summary: The AfD is far ahead in the polls in Saxony-Anhalt. But Schulze is determined to keep the AfD from becoming the first far-right party since World War II to lead a German state government.

image.caption: Saxony-Anhalt's State Premier Sven Schulze, of the conservative CDU party, hopes to to stay in office after the state election on September 6Image: Peter Gercke/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: "It's far from decided." State Premier Sven Schulze likes to repeat his big campaign message over and over again ahead of the impending election in the eastern German state of Saxony-Anhalt on September 6. His audience, however, rarely responds with enthusiasm.

The German public and international media alike are watching this election closely. Never before has the Alternative for Germany (AfD) — classified by the domestic intelligence agency as "confirmed right-wing extremist" — had a better chance to take over a state government. The party is polling at over 40% compared to Schulze's center-right Christian Democratic Union (CDU) at around 23%.

Schulze is hoping the AfD will stay below 50% and so be unable to secure a majority in the state parliament — and, with no other party willing to join it in a coalition, the AfD would be unable to form a government. That would leave it up to Schulze to form a coalition, perhaps with as many as three partners, and remain in office.
"We are fighting for every single voter right now," he told DW on August 7.
CDU's Saxony-Anhalt candidate warns against AfD taking power
Family man, engineer, cyclist
Schulze was just 11 years old at the time of German reunification. Now, at 47, the qualified industrial engineer and father of three is the youngest of Germany's 16 state premiers.

He only took over leadership of the state at the end of January, when his predecessor, Reiner Haseloff — then 71 — retired after nearly 15 years in office. The early handover to Schulze was supposed to improve the younger man's prospects in the state election. After all, a sitting premier is said to enjoy an "incumbency bonus."

Schulze is now touring the state of 2 million inhabitants. On some days, he has been seen out and about on his bicycle, complete with cycling jersey and helmet, handing out ice cream on hot summer days, and engaging in small group discussions.

Aware that his party leader, Chancellor Friedrich Merz, is not exactly popular in Germany right now, one of his recurring messages has been that he is not there "to sell the Berlin government's ideas to Saxony-Anhalt." Instead, he said, his task is "to bring issues from Saxony-Anhalt to Berlin." Not everyone in Merz's government is necessarily pleased about this message.
Celebrities welcome, Chancellor Merz not so much

This became particularly evident when Schulze appeared at campaign events in the state's larger cities alongside Dieter Hallervorden — an actor and comedian who is a household name in Germany, and who was born in Dessau in Saxony-Anhalt nearly 91 years ago.

Hallervorden, not previously known as a CDU supporter, has now joined Schulze on stage during the election campaign four times. The venues were packed, and the events easily ranked among the best-attended of Schulze's campaign.

The comedian showed no compunctions about criticizing the federal government's defense and arms export policies. During one of his musical performances, an image of protesters bearing a banner with the slogan "Stop the genocide in Gaza" was briefly visible in the background.

Schulze calmly rejected sharp criticism of Hallervorden's involvement from his party's headquarters in Berlin. He maintained that he did not share, and even rejected some of Hallervorden's views, but had shared the stage with him to demonstrate his commitment to freedom of speech. The AfD, Schulze noted, seeks to abolish freedom of speech, while he does not.
AfD a threat to German culture, says Schulze

Dessau is known around the world as being one of the homes of the Bauhaus movement, which propelled art and architecture into the modern era starting in 1919. The Nazis sought to stifle the movement when they took power in 1933.

Now, more than 90 years later, some members of the AfD have again been directly echoing the Nazis' language about the famous movement. In a speech to the state parliament last year, AfD representative Hans-Thomas Tillschneider described Bauhaus as a "wrong track of modernism" — a direct quote from the 1928 book "Art and Race" by architecture critic Paul Schultze-Naumburg, who influenced Nazi thought.
Schulze has accused the AfD of wanting to return to Germany's past eras of oppression, and sought to tie the far-right party to East Germany's communist dictatorship.

"When the AfD sings the GDR anthem at the end of its party events, it shows exactly what it wants: a return to the days of the GDR," Schulze told DW. "And I do not want us to wall ourselves in again, as happened here before. That is not what the people want."
What if Germany's far-right AfD party wins in Saxony-Anhalt?
Running a local campaign

At campaign events, Schulze has attempted to shift the focus away from federal or global political issues and toward the situation within his home state. He often cites local businesses that rely on foreign employees and on exports to worldwide markets.

Regarding healthcare and care for the elderly, he warns against simply adopting, without debate, the recommendations of a commission appointed by the federal government. That again has directly contravened Merz's message, who said that those recommendations, which some say contain several cuts to public services, should and would be followed to the letter.

But Schulze remains undeterred, and has vowed to keep discussing the issues that matter to the people of Saxony-Anhalt. "I trust the people here," he said. He added that he is counting on the people of Saxony-Anhalt to stand up against having their state "turned upside down."
At times, he gets straight to the point: this election, he says, boils down to "Sven Schulze or the AfD."
This article was originally written in German.

articles.title: Countries legally obliged to consider slavery reparations, says UN committee
articles.summary:
Guidance says states must implement ‘comprehensive measures’ to address legacy of racial discrimination

A UN committee has said countries are legally obliged to consider reparations for the…

blocks.text: A UN committee has said countries are legally obliged to consider reparations for the transatlantic slave trade and take other ⁠measures to address the enduring ⁠legacy of racial ​discrimination.

Guidance published on Monday by the committee on the elimination of racial discrimination (CERD) said the obligations arose from ⁠a legally binding 1965 convention on racial discrimination, not from the legal standards that existed when the slave trade took place.
The committee described the approach as a “paradigm ⁠shift” away from debates over historical responsibility that have often been used by governments to resist reparations ​claims.
“States parties must implement comprehensive reparatory measures for ‌people of African descent, ‌covering all aspects of remedies,” said the UN document, which may be cited in courtrooms.
At least 12.5 ‌million Africans were taken and sold between the 15th and 19th centuries in what CERD called the largest forced displacement in history.

Calls for reparations – ranging from official apologies to financial compensation – have gained momentum internationally, though opponents argue states and institutions should not be held responsible for historical crimes. The EU and Britain abstained from a UN resolution ‌on slavery in March.
Some states have sought to dodge claims for justice in courtrooms by arguing that there were no international laws outlawing the slave trade ​at the time – the so-called intertemporality principle.

But the UN document argues that, regardless of whether slavery and the slave trade were illegal under the laws of the day, countries remain responsible under current international obligations to tackle their continuing effects.

“Irrespective of the legal characterisation of the original historical acts, states parties remain bound ⁠by their present obligations under the convention to address structural inequalities,” the UN document ​says.
Financial compensation alone is ​not sufficient, it adds, urging “transformative” measures including ​opening archives, revising public memorials and establishing independent truth commissions.
after newsletter promotion
Pela Boker Wilson, a committee expert ​from Liberia who helped draft ‌the document, said ​she expected states ​to move beyond broad expressions of regret and review policies and laws.

“We are calling on state parties to take concrete and meaningful action,” she told Reuters. “We want to affirm the dignity of those whose suffering was denied, whose suffering was minimised or forgotten.”

articles.title: Morocco not to blame for Ceuta border breach, says Spanish PM
articles.summary:
Pedro Sánchez says two countries are cooperating after mass incursion by 70,000 people into north African enclave

Spain’s prime minister, Pedro Sánchez, has insisted there was no evidence…

blocks.text: Spain’s prime minister, Pedro Sánchez, has insisted there was no evidence to suggest the Moroccan government was behind last month’s massive border crossing into Ceuta.

As many as 141 people are thought to have died trying to enter the Spanish enclave at the end of July. The influx of about 70,000 men, women and children unleashed a political crisis, a humanitarian emergency and reignited tensions over immigration within the EU.
Although the overwhelming majority of the migrants crossed back into Morocco weeks ago, hundreds of people, including minors, are still on the streets of Ceuta, leading to tensions with residents.

Despite speculation that Rabat may have engineered the mass crossing as a means of showing its displeasure at Spain’s rapprochement with Algeria, Sánchez said there was nothing to indicate the involvement of the Moroccan authorities.
“There’s no information from any intelligence agency that raises doubts over the involvement of Moroccan authorities,” he told Cadena Ser radio on Monday.

“Cooperation with Morocco is frankly positive. I’d like to stress that we need to be aware that this crisis can be resolved only through cooperation – and not through a lack of trust in Morocco, which would only further aggravate the already complex situation we have in Ceuta.”

The prime minister once again pointed the finger at “criminal gangs” who had used disinformation to falsely claim that a ruling by Spain’s supreme court meant that no one who entered Ceuta by swimming could be deported back to Morocco.

He also said fake news had been pumped out on social media accounts “associated with Russia, Israel and the international far right that always use migration to attack not just Spain but also Europe”.
Sánchez said that about 1,500 migrants remained in Ceuta, of whom 1,200 are minors, and there would soon be “sufficient capacity” to accommodate all those still in the enclave.

Their continuing presence has led to clashes between some Ceuta residents and police, while some of the migrants have had their belongings burned while sleeping rough on beaches. On Saturday, four Moroccan migrants were arrested for throwing stones at Spanish soldiers.

Spain’s conservative People’s party has accused the government of failing to protect the people of Ceuta. “It did nothing to avoid the invasion on 30 July and it’s doing nothing to stop the public order crisis that’s getting worse every day,” the PP’s leader, Alberto Núñez Feijóo, said last week.

Santiago Abascal, the leader of the far-right Vox party, has described events in Ceuta as “an invasion and an act of war promoted by Morocco and allowed by Sánchez, who is incapable of responding because he is subservient to Morocco”.

articles.title: Inside the sea cucumber smuggling boom
articles.summary: A quiet multimillion‑dollar black market is exploding across the Indian Ocean, driven by one unlikely animal: the sea cucumber.

image.caption: Sea cucumbers are neither cucumbers nor fish, but invertebrate marine animals with a skin or hard coveringImage: oceansasia.org

blocks.text: When it comes to smuggling, squishy sea blobs that spend their lives eating and pooping are probably not what comes to mind. But a group of lumpen creatures known as sea cucumbers are at the center of a $200 million (€175 million) black market trade.

Known alternately and misleadingly as sea cucumbers or sand fish, they are actually neither cucumbers nor fish, but echinoderms. In other words, invertebrate marine animals with a skin or a hard covering.

Found in abundance around the Andaman Islands — the easternmost landmass of the Indian territory— local biologist Sangamesh Uday says they are so ecologically important that without them the intertidal zone "wouldn't be an ecosystem, it would just be broken rocks."

blocks.caption: Sea cucumbers are crucial for the local ecosystem, says local biologist  Uday Image: Parinmnpa/Dreamstime/IMAGO

blocks.text: The 1500 or so species of sea cucumber around the world are great marine recyclers. They eat organic material including bacteria and microalgae, break it down, and excrete clean oxygenated sand. This keeps vital nutrients like nitrogen and phosphorous in circulation and suppresses coral diseases.

It also boosts ocean alkalinity levels which helps to slow down acidification — which is becoming a huge issue as rising levels of greenhouse gases in the atmosphere cause oceans to warm. In short, it's hard to overstate the environmental importance of these innocuous looking lumps.
Why are they being smuggled?

To their detriment, sea cucumbers are also considered a delicacy, especially in China and Southeast Asia. Yet historical records show their trade between Indonesian fishers and Chinese traders even 800 years ago.

They are used in soups, served as pickled sides or turned into traditional medicine. And though there is some scientific evidence that the Omega-3 they contain is a useful antioxidant and anti-inflammatory, they're mostly popular because they're quite phallic — and therefore considered an aphrodisiac.

blocks.caption: Sea cucumbers are considered a delicacy, used in soups or used as traditional medicineImage: oceansasia.org

blocks.text: Since the 1980s, commercial sea cucumber harvesting has expanded globally — with better access as well as higher incomes and demand in East Asia acting as the main drivers. Though many countries have outlawed the practice, some like Sri Lanka and Madagascar do allow fishing and aquaculture. Of the existing sea cucumber fisheries, 70% have become overexploited globally.

The combination of the increasing demand and legal complexities, has drawn the attention of minor and major mafias. Some of the largest Mexican cartels and even the Japanese Yakuza have been reported as diversifying their portfolios and using sea cucumbers and other related sea creatures to keep the money flowing.
These illicit groups enter every aspect of the supply chain — from extorting fishermen to the final smuggling of illegally-caught cucumbers across borders.

They exploit weak environmental regulations and a lack of official knowledge around rules and species. Sea cucumbers are sometimes marked as legal fish consignments or smuggled into countries that do allow trade in the species.
Leading expert on sea cucumber crime, Teale Phelps Bondaroff, says awareness is critical in dealing with the issue.
"While many law enforcement officers may be on the lookout for drugs, weapons, or well-known wildlife contraband like ivory, rhino horns, or shark fins, sea cucumbers may slip past," he told DW.
Poachers from overseas drawn to the Andaman Islands
The Indian government began regulating sea cucumbers in the 1980s and introduced a blanket ban on fishing them in 2001, when it saw the impact of the illicit trade on local populations.

Since then, India has become the country with the strongest protections for the species. Anyone who catches one faces a seven-year jail term — the same sentence handed down for poaching a tiger or elephant.

As a result, sea cucumbers close to the Andaman Islands have generally thrived. In the ocean around Myanmar, around 50km (30 miles) further north, it's a different picture. Civil war in the country has severely impacted local livelihoods and local black-market agents are using the instability to offer comparatively higher sums for a boatload of illegally caught sea cucumbers. And as their numbers in local waters dwindle, poachers head south.
It is no easy game, however. They have to dodge the Indian coast guard, navy, police, evade local fishermen and even dense populations of crocodiles.
Inside the $200 million black market for... sea cucumbers?!

They survive on fish, freediving using hookah pipes to breathe, and spend months rationing their diesel to ensure they have enough to make it back home — evading the Myanmar authorities and pirates looking to try and steal their catch.

Many poachers are caught by the regional Andaman and Nicobar police, who are being specifically trained to comb the mangrove islands to find them. At least 50 people have been arrested in the past year, some as young as 16 and some in their 60s. And some who have come back for the second or third time — at risk of being incarcerated again, after completing full sentences.
Is there a way to stop the illegal trade?
Despite the efforts of the Indian authorities, the number of poachers coming in, year after year, has stayed stable.

Bondaroff sees a need to sound the alarm at a global level. Other similar trades, like that of shark fins, have been slowed thanks to increased awareness about its cruelty and impact on the ecosystem — making it less socially acceptable.
"The solution must include educating consumers about the harms of unsustainable and illegal sea cucumber extraction and tackling seafood fraud."

blocks.caption: Poachers often hide on mangrove islands in the Andamans, making it hard to catch themImage: Dheeraj Aithal/DW

blocks.text: Other suggestions include India opening up small areas of its waters where sea cucumbers can be legally fished. Or introducing community-based aquaculture that is easier to regulate and would also benefit local fishers.
But Bondaroff says tackling the problem also requires cooperation and a deep understanding of the issue.
"This means liaising and information sharing between governments and law enforcement agencies," he said. "And working together to address the complex financial crimes that enable sea cucumber crime."
This report was supported by the Pulitzer Center.

articles.title: Bhutan hosts first ‘conscious food summit’ amid threats to global food systems
articles.summary:
Organisers say world must revive its spiritual relationship with food as climate crisis and conflict disrupt food security

Mending the broken food system under the threat of climate-driven…

blocks.text: Mending the broken food system under the threat of climate-driven weather extremes will require more than economic fixes and intensive agriculture, according to the organisers of a pioneering summit this week, who say the world must revive its spiritual relationship with food.

Delegates from more than 60 countries and the UN will gather for the next five days in Paro in the tiny Himalayan nation of Bhutan for the world’s first “conscious food summit”, which will bring together governments and farmers, mindfulness experts and yoga therapists.

Tshering Tobgay, Bhutan’s prime minister, said: “Food lies at the intersection of many of the defining challenges of our time – hunger, poor nutrition, poverty, climate change, biodiversity loss, and increasingly food security is also being disrupted by conflict and geopolitical instability. Our central message is simple: transforming our food systems requires both inner and outer change.”

Conscious eating is at the heart of these talks, which will promote regenerative practices and Indigenous knowledge. “Consciousness can cultivate compassion, empathy, resilience, creativity and a stronger connection with nature,” Tobgay said in an interview with the Guardian. “This does not mean choosing spirituality over science. It means recognising that our values and mindsets influence how science, policy, finance and technology are used.”

blocks.caption: Tshering Tobgay: ‘Food systems are ultimately shaped by human choices.’ Photograph: Mike Bowers/The Guardian

blocks.text: The impacts of the climate crisis have been brought home close to Bhutan’s borders with the disaster in its near neighbour Nepal last week where a glacial collapse led to floods and landslides that killed hundreds.

This year and next as the “super El Niño” hits, the World Food Programme has warned that 50 million people could be pushed close to starvation. Food shortages and higher prices for staples are likely around the world. It follows a summer in the northern hemisphere in which harvests have been devastated by drought, intense heat and wildfires.

Jerry Spooner, of Regenerative Vanua, a Pacific NGO, said the threats would push global food systems to their limit. “As we face the growing impacts of climate change, a potential super El Niño, biodiversity loss and increasing global instability, it is becoming clear that our food systems are not resilient enough for the challenges ahead,” he said. “The opportunity in Bhutan is to move beyond discussing how we produce more food and instead focus on how we build food systems that regenerate ecosystems, strengthen communities, celebrate culture and improve our collective resilience.”

blocks.caption: Cows searching for food in a pasture in Tecoluca, El Salvador, where the lack of rainfall has reduced the availability of grass and other forage for livestock. Photograph: Marvin Recinos/AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: Tobgay said people must articulate the values they wanted to see reflected in the way food is produced and consumed, instead of relying on businesses and governments to shape food choices. “Food systems are ultimately shaped by human choices, institutions, incentives, relationships and values,” he said. “So we must address root causes as well as symptoms.”
Farmers and rural people were often at the mercy of markets and global forces. “Too often, policies are developed for these groups rather than with them,” Tobgay said.
after newsletter promotion

The summit will focus not on bombastic political speeches and promises but on fostering inner change, with the help of “spiritual masters” such as mindfulness practitioners. Food had become a commodity on world markets and was treated carelessly as a result, leading to waste and unhealthy eating, and those attitudes must be reversed, Tobgay said.

“Outer change is agriculture, markets, finance, public policy and consumption,” he said. “Consciousness has value only if it influences our decisions and changes how we act. For example, a conscious approach to production would care for both the land and the farmer. It would regenerate soils, not deplete them. It would protect water. It would reduce pollution and deforestation and recognise the dignity and wellbeing of the people who produce the food that sustain us.”

Tobgay begins each day at 5am with a bowl of porridge and a banana, eaten sitting by a small stream that runs near his house. “I listen to the birds that are up and about by that time, I listen to the stream and the water,” he said.

Anyone could try conscious eating, he added. Many cultures have a tradition before meals of reflecting on the food, its provenance and preparation, and giving thanks. Reviving such practices would take almost no time but could, he hopes, be one of the first steps to a revolution in the way we treat the planet and each other.

articles.title: Iran hostilities flare after US strike in strait of Hormuz; supertanker hits mines and catches fire – Middle East crisis live
articles.summary: US targets Iran’s Larak Island in first exchange of fire in more than a month, sparking reprisals against US forces in Jordan and UAE

blocks.text: US and Iran trade strikes for first time in a month
Welcome to our live coverage as hostilities between the US and Iran flared again for the first time in a month, with American strikes on Iran prompting retaliation from Tehran.

A supertanker caught ⁠fire and was brought to a complete ⁠halt after ⁠hitting two naval mines in ⁠the southern strait of Hormuz, Iran state ⁠TV reported on Monday, ​citing ‌a statement ‌from the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps.

The IRGC said the tanker had been attempting to pass through the waterway illegally. It ‌did not identify the vessel or provide information ​about its crew. It warned that other ships violating ⁠its security rules would face ​the ​same fate and ​said compliance with ​its regulations ‌for ​passage ​through the strait was mandatory.

On Sunday, the US said it carried out airstrikes on Iranian rocket launchers on Larak Island in the strait, with an American official saying the IRGC was preparing to launch rockets with sea mines into the narrow waterway.

The IRGC said on Monday it attacked two US military airbases with ballistic missiles in Washington-allied Jordan, causing “heavy damage”, state media reported. Jordan’s army said it had intercepted eight missiles, without stating their origin.

Iran said later it had targeted US military personnel at an airbase in the United Arab Emirates. Donald Trump later claimed on social media that Iran’s energy hub of Kharg Island was “being blown to smithereens”.
In other developments:

items: Iran’s supreme leader called the US and Israel enemies of all Islamic nations. In a written message issued six months on from the start of the war, Ayatollah Mojtaba Khamenei also urged rulers of Muslim nations to “know your real enemy, understand its plans and confront it”, the official Irna news agency reported.

Israel’s Shin Bet security agency says it urgently evacuated prime minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s oldest son from the US due to a threat against him. In a brief statement the Associated Press obtained on Sunday, the Shin Bet confirmed there had been a “significant threat” to Yair Netanyahu, without elaborating.
US treasury secretary Scott Bessent will step up efforts to isolate Iran economically as he hosts G20 counterparts this week, a US official has said.

Iranian president Masoud Pezeshkian is due to take part in a summit starting on Monday of the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation, a regional bloc that seeks to be a counter-influence to the west. Russia’s Vladimir Putin is expected to hold separate bilateral talks with Pezeshkian and China’s Xi Jinping, among other leaders, a Kremlin spokesperson said.

blocks.text: Key events

items: 23m agoHead of National Iranian Oil Company dismisses Trump’s claim of Kharg Island attack

blocks.text: Head of National Iranian Oil Company dismisses Trump’s claim of Kharg Island attack

Hours after the attacks, the US president, Donald Trump, claimed in a social media post – featuring an AI video showing oil infrastructure exploding – that Iran’s energy hub of Kharg island was being “blown to smithereens”, without any supporting evidence.
Hamid Bovard, ⁠CEO of ⁠the ​National Iranian Oil Company, mocked Trump’s post, saying that oil operations there are continuing.

“Trump’s tweets are laughable and conditions in Kharg are calm and appropriate,” Nournews cited him as ‌saying, adding that the island had been bombed repeatedly by US and Israeli ⁠forces in the past, but oil ​workers ​had not ​allowed operations to stop “even ​for ‌a moment”.
Kharg Island is a major Iranian energy hub responsible for handling about 90% of Iran’s crude oil exports, making it among the country’s most sensitive economic targets.

Trump has previously threatened to seize the island, which hosts vast storage facilities, but has rowed back on his threats, perhaps knowing that any takeover would require the US to put boots on the ground, exposing American forces to Iranian attacks.

articles.title: Monday briefing: Nepal and Tibet’s floods are a warning for the future
articles.summary:
In today’s newsletter: As rescuers search for survivors after catastrophic floods, the disaster offers a stark warning about the climate risks facing the region, and the world

Good morning.…

blocks.text: Good morning. Over the weekend, rescue workers in Nepal and Tibet raced to find people who are still trapped in villages affected by catastrophic flash floods. As of this morning, the death toll stands at 903, and more than 4,000 people are missing.

For those of you reading this in a place where life continues as usual, the scale of devastation is hard to fathom. In a matter of minutes, a torrent of mud and debris engulfed entire villages, snapped bridges and swept away people’s homes and families. Some survivors are marooned on top of buildings that rescue workers can’t reach. Others are trapped in tunnels beneath the ground. Many have no idea if their loved ones are still alive.

The floods exemplify a wider threat. The delicate processes that have shaped our climate for centuries are unwinding at a terrifying pace. Scientists are still investigating the precise sequence of events that caused these floods, but as the planet heats up and glaciers melt, events like this will keep happening.

The Guardian has been covering the floods extensively – you can read our visual guide to the disaster, and our latest report on it here. For this morning’s newsletter, I spoke to our south Asia correspondent Hannah Ellis-Petersen, who is on the ground in Kathmandu. She’s been speaking to survivors and reporting on the rescue operation since Thursday. That’s after the headlines.
Weekend roundup

items: UK politics | PC Andrew Harper’s killers will remain in prison after Andy Burnham announced changes to the early release scheme that will see anyone convicted of unlawful killing, including all forms of manslaughter, excluded from the scheme.

Milo Yiannopoulos | Far-right British media provocateur Milo Yiannopoulos has been deported from the US back to the UK by Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) in connection with what the agency said was expired authorisation to be in the country.

US-Iran | Iran has launched retaliatory strikes on airbases in Jordan after the United States attacked Iranian rocket launchers on an island in the strait of Hormuz, the first such strikes in a month.
Iceland | In a blow to Brussels, Iceland has held a referendum that has narrowly ⁠rejected ⁠the government’s proposal ​to hold ⁠accession talks with ⁠the ​EU.

Nepal-Tibet disaster | A headteacher in Nepal evacuated 900 children from a school moments before a deadly wall of water struck their town amid the devastating flash floods that have killed almost 800 people and left thousands missing.

blocks.text: In depth: An ‘absolute catastrophe’

blocks.caption: ‘Everything was either submerged in mud, or mangled’  Photograph: cnsphoto/Reuters

blocks.text: At 8:37am on Wednesday morning, an enormous chunk of ice from a glacier in the Himalayas broke off and crashed on to a mountain near the border between Nepal and Tibet. It caused a fearsome avalanche of ice and rock, which surged downstream into the Bhotekoshi and Trishuli rivers, submerging villages and sweeping roads away.

At first, the scale of damage was unclear. Nepal is prone to natural disasters, and many of the villages affected by these floods are extremely remote. Early satellite images of the region were obscured by thick clouds of dust, and scientists initially assumed that an earthquake must have caused the flood, rather than a glacier collapse. By Wednesday night, as more images and reports emerged, it became clear that the floods were an “absolute catastrophe,” Hannah says. On Thursday, she boarded a flight to Kathmandu, the capital city near the destruction.

When Hannah arrived in Bidur, a small city two hours from Kathmandu, on Friday morning, most of its buildings had been destroyed, their carcasses exposed like matchsticks. A team of rescue workers in yellow hard hats were working to clear the roads. “There was a bank, an ATM machine, and a truck that was lying on its side,” she says. “Everything else was either submerged in mud, or mangled.”
The race to save lives

The Nepali army has been organising the rescue operation from a military base in Bidur. Large sections of the road that links Bidur to villages higher in the valley have been washed away, so rescues are happening by air, and the sound of helicopters is nearly constant. Every two to three minutes, a chopper lands, deposits survivors, and sets off again. The mud is so thick in some places that helicopters have struggled to land. Rasuwa, an area where entire villages were destroyed, was still inaccessible when I spoke to Hannah on Sunday afternoon. “The ground zero of the floods has still not been reached by journalists, and is only just being reached by the army,” she says.

Hundreds, if not thousands, of people have been rescued, and hundreds of people are now waiting outside the army base in Bidur scanning lists of survivors posted on the walls. At hospitals in Kathmandu, health workers have put up photos of bodies that are so disfigured their families have struggled to identify them. Authorities have begun burying human remains because there isn’t enough mortuary space to prevent them from decomposing. “I’ve spoken to people who have up to 12 relatives who have gone missing,” says Hannah, who visited hospitals in Kathmandu on Saturday. “And there’s no phone signal in the more remote villages. So another big cause of suffering is this huge uncertainty.”
Thousands still missing

So far there are 4,247 people who are missing, according to Nepal’s disaster agency (592 of whom are foreigners, including 43 Australians, and 48 from the UK, including 15 reported missing in China). Among them are 933 workers from Nepal and neighbouring countries who were working on hydroelectric power projects along the river. These rely on vast tunnel systems that are built deep into the ground, and rescue teams have to dig through mud and bore through tunnel walls to extricate trapped workers. On Saturday, the Nepali army had a small breakthrough when it successfully inserted a pipe into a tunnel at a hydroelectric site in Trishuli, allowing air to be pumped into the tunnel. In the early hours this morning, rescue efforts were “intensified” at the site, with a team of 90 people deployed.

The army is racing against time to rescue the living. “People are stuck in areas that have no drinking water, or access to food. They’re completely cut off,” Hannah says. The picture of devastation has emerged more quickly in Nepal than in Tibet, where the Chinese government retains a tight grip on information. On Friday, as the official death toll in Nepal rose to 538 people, China estimated that just five people had died in Tibet. The Chinese authorities have since revised their numbers, and estimate that at least 16 people are dead and 546 missing.
The long road to recovery

It will take months to clear away the mud, and some people will never find their relatives’ bodies. Some were pushed so far down the river that they have washed up in India. “People have lost everything,” says Hannah. “I saw one woman clutching a bottle of cooking oil, because it’s the only thing she had left.” Climate stories in the global south often struggle to break through, so it’s encouraging that these floods have been covered so widely. But when the news cycle has moved on, Nepal will be left with the enormous task of rebuilding. It estimates that cost could be between $4bn to $5bn, almost a tenth of its economy.

“It’s getting increasingly difficult for Nepal to pick itself up,” Hannah tells me. In Kathmandu, buildings destroyed by the 2015 earthquake, which killed nearly 9,000 people, are still in ruins. The EU has committed €2m to Nepal to help with the floods, and Britain has committed £5m. There’s also been a lot of focus on the need for better early monitoring systems. All of this matters. But as Sunil Acharya, a climate policy specialist based in Kathmandu, wrote in this interesting Opinion column, it also obscures a more fundamental problem: systems to monitor these events were designed for yesterday’s risks, not today’s extremes. Nepal’s warning systems were destroyed before they could alert people near the source of the flood.

Looming over all this is the fact that nations like Nepal, which has contributed a minuscule amount to historic greenhouse gas emissions, will suffer the worst effects of the climate crisis. It needs far more assistance to cope with the consequences of richer nations’ actions. And it needs those nations to rapidly cut their emissions, before the crisis gets worse.
The week to come

A bit of good news to remind you that the world’s not all bad

blocks.caption: The number of people living with dementia around the world is forecast to nearly triple to 153 million by 2050. Photograph: Joe Giddens/PA

blocks.text: Results from a 15-year study suggest that statins, the cholesterol-busting drugs, can lower the risk of dementia by 15%. In the largest study of its kind, researchers tracked more than 132,000 people in Denmark between 2006 and 2021. Those who started on statins during the study period were 10% less likely to develop dementia. Those taking them early reduced their risk by 15%. The results were similar in women and men. The number of people living with dementia globally is forecast to nearly triple to 153 million by 2050. But, experts believe almost half of dementia cases could be prevented or delayed.

articles.title: Humanitarian crisis worsening in refuge for civilians fleeing Sudan’s civil war
articles.summary:
Conditions are deteriorating in city of El Obeid and camps on its outskirts, with more people arriving every day

Humanitarian conditions in the Sudanese city of El Obeid and two camps on its…

blocks.text: Humanitarian conditions in the Sudanese city of El Obeid and two camps on its outskirts are dire and deteriorating, according to people on the ground, as civilians displaced by fighting between the Sudanese Armed Forces and Rapid Support Forces (RSF) militia continue to pour in from the surrounding countryside.

The UN says more than 15,000 families have arrived since mid-July, joining more than 200,000 people who arrived in the first half of the year, according to government figures cited by Save the Children.

“The situation is very harsh and is deteriorating as El Obeid is receiving IDPs [internally displaced people] on a daily basis … The city is shockingly overcrowded,” said Maryam, a humanitarian volunteer whose name has been changed for her safety.
The new arrivals came on foot, carrying almost nothing, she said. “They also suffer from a shortage of food and they definitely arrive traumatised.”
The city, the capital of North Kordofan province, was home to around half a million people before the war broke out more than three years ago.

blocks.caption: Tens of thousands of people are living in tented camps around El Obeid.  Photograph: AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: While many of the new arrivals have been absorbed into the city, tens of thousands are living in two main tented camps. According to analysis of satellite data by the Yale Humanitarian Research Lab, 800 new tents appeared in one of the camps between 4 and 25 August.

“During my visit, I saw 450 arrivals coming from the surrounding villages just that morning,” said Paul Byars, the Sudan country director for the Danish Refugee Council, who was in El Obeid last week. “The authorities’ estimates are correct, that 85% of them are women and children. Most of the men are staying behind because this is the only time for farming.”
Civil war erupted in Sudan’s capital, Khartoum, about 250 miles (400km) north-east of El Obeid, on 15 April 2023, when a power struggle between the armed forces and RSF descended into open conflict.
Since then, about 11.3 million people have been displaced, more than a fifth of the population. Some parts of the country, including El Obeid and surrounding areas, are at risk of famine.

Estimates of the number of people killed in the war range from tens to hundreds of thousands. More than 10,000 people are thought to have been massacred by the RSF in El Fasher over two days when they seized the city in Sudan’s western Darfur region in October 2025 after an 18-month siege.

blocks.caption: The damaged interior of a lawyers' syndicate in El Obeid, reportedly targeted by the RSF in July. Photograph: AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: A surge in RSF drone strikes on El Obeid and nearby areas in June led the UN to warn that the city could face a repeat of what happened in El Fasher.

The number of strikes has since fallen. The armed forces also recaptured a key road leading north to Khartoum in late July, which at least partly lifted the threat of besiegement. However, drones are still killing and injuring civilians, while violence rages in the surrounding districts, pushing people to the city.

Recently, volunteers in El Obeid had noticed more “double-tap” drone strikes, where a second drone follows the first, hitting rescuers at the scene, Maryam said. “It is hard, so hard, living with this, hearing the sound of a drone hitting somewhere,” she said. “It’s very disturbing.”

Sudan’s civil war has become dominated by drones, accounting for half of all violent incidents, up from 4% at the start of the war, said Nohad Eltayeb, who monitors Sudan for Acled, a conflict tracking group.
Both sides used drones, but the RSF’s usage had become more volatile since the US war with Iran began to interrupt supply lines in February, she said. “They rely on fewer, very targeted strikes.”

So far this year, there have been 322 incidents of violence affecting civilians in the wider Kordofan region, compared with 388 for the whole of 2025, according to Acled data. While the RSF was responsible for half of those, the SAF has also killed and injured civilians. On 10 August, armed forces and an allied militia killed five civilians and injured 10 about 60 miles north-east of El Obeid, according to Emergency Lawyers, a non-governmental group.

With the threats to delivery trucks, food prices have rocketed. In north Kordofan in July, according to World Food Programme data, a litre of groundnut oil cost 17,000 Sudanese pounds (£21), up from 13,000 in June and 7,700 a year ago. The prices of wheat flour and goat and sheep meat have also more than doubled in the last year.

blocks.caption: Conditions in the camps around El Obeid are said to be poor.  Photograph: AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: Meanwhile, El Obeid’s power and water infrastructure still has not fully recovered from RSF drone strikes in June.

“The main problem is the big [water] source that is in the north of the city has been severely damaged and it has not been repaired,” said Esperanza Santos, an emergency coordinator in Sudan for Médecins Sans Frontières. “The water pipes in the city have [also] been impacted. So mostly, both in the city – for example, in the hospital – and also in the IDP camps, they are relying on water trucking and it’s not enough.”

Conditions in the camps were poor too, Santos said. “In terms of sanitation, it’s very, very bad. It’s not enough. The ratio of latrines per person is impossible – there are more than 100 people for a latrine. So basically there is open defecation.”

Maryam said she and her fellow local volunteers remained committed, despite the difficulties. “The situation is deteriorating, but we are trying to stay together, to stay strong in the face of the drone attacks and the influx of IDPs … We are living with this and we hope things will become better.”

articles.title: Canada's cadets condemn Pete Hegseth's 'unacceptable' post

image.caption: Secretary of War Pete Hegseth speaks during an event in Arlington, Va., on Aug. 26 to honour Marines. (Andrew Harnik/Getty Images)

blocks.text: World
The U.S. Pentagon is standing behind a controversial social media post by War Secretary Pete Hegseth about a Canadian cadet program.
U.S. Pentagon defends controversial post by war secretary
· The Canadian Press
· Posted: Sep 01, 2026 11:46 AM EDT | Last Updated: 2 minutes ago
The Pentagon is standing behind a controversial social media post by U.S. War Secretary Pete Hegseth about a Canadian cadet program.
Hegseth on Monday posted an image from the Cadet Training Centre in Vernon, B.C., depicting two young women in uniform with the caption "this is real" alongside a Canadian flag.
The online response to Hegseth's post was filled with remarks belittling the physical appearance of the people in the photo, but it also triggered massive backlash from Canadians.

Some people posted that it was unfair for Hegseth to target the youth program in an attempt to disparage the Canadian Armed Forces and others criticized him for body-shaming women serving in the cadet program.
🇨🇦 (this is real) pic.twitter.com/Ucx2FNdi1q—PeteHegseth
Asked about the backlash today, Pentagon deputy press secretary Jacob Bliss said "the X post speaks for itself."
Cadets blast Hegseth post
The Army Cadet League of Canada condemned the online harassment and mockery of cadets and their achievements.
"Directing derogatory commentary toward youth who are actively working to better themselves and serve their communities is unacceptable," the league said about Hegseth's remarks in a statement.

It said the league "stands firmly behind cadets, adult staff, volunteers, and officers who dedicate their time to building stronger communities and developing the next generation of Canadian leaders."

items: Canada ready to further distance itself from U.S. on military procurement
Carney says Trump and his cabinet should stop 'throwing shade' and get serious about a deal

blocks.text: The national, community-based cadet program is for youth aged 12 to 18. A federal government website says the program provides "opportunities for youth to gain valuable knowledge and skills that build confidence and help pave the way in a transition to adulthood."

It's not clear how exactly the cadet training program's Instagram account — which had 1,821 followers as of Tuesday morning — came onto Hegseth's radar. Bliss, who works in the office of the assistant to the secretary of war for public affairs, did not respond to questions about how the defence secretary became aware of it.
When asked by reporters in Ottawa today about the post from Hegseth, Prime Minister Mark Carney said the message was "beneath their office."

"When the Americans stop doing memes, stop throwing shade, stop trying to be tough and start being serious about having the discussions, we can have those discussions," he said. "But it's not constructive, but that's their democracy."
B.C. Premier David Eby said Hegseth's post and the Pentagon's defence of it were an embarrassment.
"It tells you everything you need to know about the amateur-hour, distracted, bizarre leadership that Americans are being subjected to," Eby said.
He cited an ongoing military conference in Victoria, which includes U.S. representatives, as an example of the importance of co-operation during "unstable times."

Hegseth's post was also condemned by Arizona Democratic Sen. Ruben Gallego, a U.S. Marine Corps veteran, who called the comments "stupid" and "really deeply disrespectful to the men and women of Canada that have died fighting with us."
Hegseth's comments on Canadian military 'stupid,' says U.S. Democratic senator
Comments come amid trade tensions
The post comes as tensions between Canada and the United States increased after trade talks broke down last month.
The Trump administration hit Canada with 50 per cent tariffs on an array of goods in August, with both countries blaming the other for adding last-minute changes during negotiations.
Canada is set to implement its retaliatory duties next week.

items: America 'not at war' with Canada, insists U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent

blocks.text: Trump has spent the weeks since talks were frozen incessantly targeting Canada in his public remarks and social media posts. Last week, he signed an executive order to change the name of Lake Ontario to "Lake America" in his latest effort to agitate America's northern neighbour.
Many in Trump's team have turned their insults to Canada's military. U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent on Monday told CNBC the U.S. isn't at war with Canada.
"What are they going to do, take their two submarines from the Edmonton mall and sic them on us?" Bessent said.
Trump official mocks Canada, insists there's no trade war
The week prior, U.S. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy claimed on Fox News that Canada "doesn't have a military."

Conservative MP Garnett Genuis responded to Hegseth's post on Monday saying "cadets do great work, and are not members of the military." He added that "158 members of the Canadian military gave their lives in Afghanistan after your country was attacked."
"Canada and the U.S. have a great history of fighting together for freedom and justice. It's history worth remembering," Genuis said.

Hegseth is facing immense pressure domestically from an unpopular and escalating war with Iran, the closure of the Strait of Hormuz, depleting stockpiles of munitions and the departure of top military figures during his tenure.
In the latest series of shakeups of military leadership, on Monday, Army Secretary Dan Driscoll resigned following widely reported tensions with Hegseth.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR
Kelly Geraldine Malone is a journalist based in Winnipeg. She worked for CBC Manitoba and was a University of Toronto Munk School of Global Affairs Fellow in Global Journalism 2016-17.

articles.title: 6 more byelections on horizon will test Liberal momentum, pressure other parties

image.caption: Elections Canada signs are seen in Beaches-East York, one of the three ridings the Liberals won on Monday. (Keito Newman/The Canadian Press)

blocks.text: Politics·New

The Liberals are taking a victory lap after scoring a hat trick of byelection wins on Monday night — but there are still a batch of seats that need to be filled and will serve as another temperature check of the electorate in the months to come.
Carney being 'very strategic in grouping the byelections,' says political scientist
Prime Minister Mark Carney's party garnered over 50 per cent of the vote in each riding that was up for grabs on Monday, picking up seats in Ontario, B.C. and Quebec.
"The message from Canadians I think is clear. They've given their support … to the government's plan and I think that's because Canadians are united," Carney told reporters in Ottawa on Tuesday.

Lori Turnbull, a political science professor at Dalhousie University, said the Liberal wins in North Vancouver-Capilano and Beaches-East York aren't surprising given that they're considered safe Liberal seats. But she said she thinks Daniel Gobeil's win in Chicoutimi-Le Fjord was a vote of confidence in how Carney is handling the trade war with the U.S.

items: Liberals sweep 3 federal byelections in Ontario, Quebec and B.C.
Carney says Trump and his cabinet should stop 'throwing shade' and get serious about a deal

blocks.text: Turnbull said the Liberals picking Gobeil was a sign the Carney government wanted to make the byelection about the trade war.
"The fact that he chose a dairy farmer as a candidate, [signalled] a clear commitment to supply management," she said.

Three MPs resigned in the past week, which makes for five official vacancies at the moment. With Ontario Conservative Larry Brock set to step down later this month, that means six byelections will need to be held.

Conservative Cathay Wagantall officially resigned her Saskatchewan seat on Monday. Her resignation was preceded by former Liberal cabinet minister Steven Guilbeault — who officially resigned on Friday after giving notice that he was leaving back in May — and former NDP MP Alexandre Boulerice who stepped down last Tuesday to run in Quebec's provincial election.
The Bloc Québécois' Simon-Pierre Savard-Tremblay stepped down in June, also to run provincially. Liberal Shaun Chen resigned in mid-August.

Éric Grenier, author and analyst with The Writ, told CBC's Power & Politics that as things currently stand in the polls it's likely that the Liberals will keep the ridings they previously held and possibly pick up a few more.
"Still going to have lots of intrigue and interest in that next set of byelections and the Liberals will be looking to expand their majority," he told guest host John Paul Tasker.
Grenier said although Brock's riding of Brantford-Brant South-Six Nations has previously been considered a reliable Conservative seat, it will be one to watch when the campaign kicks off.
Brock won re-election in 2025 with just over 50 per cent of the vote, but the Liberals pulled in about 40 per cent. The Liberals picked up around 30 per cent in previous iterations of that riding.
"That will be a lot of pressure for [Conservative Leader] Pierre Poilievre," Grenier said.
Liberals sweep 3 federal byelections in Ontario, Quebec and B.C.

Turnbull expects the Liberals will make a push for Rosemont-La Petite-Patrie, Boulerice's former riding. The former NDP MP was the last ripple of the 2011 Orange Wave — the only New Democrat who remained in Quebec. Like in Chicoutimi-Le Fjord, Turnbull said the trade war might become a key issue in the Montreal riding.
"The Bloc and the NDP are in a really tough spot because if the question is, 'who do you want to run the country' — they are not in a position to form government," she said.
When Carney set Monday's three byelections in motion, he opted not to include Saint-Hyacinthe-Bagot-Acton.
That riding, east of Montreal, has been largely Bloc territory since the early 1990s. Turnbull said Carney avoiding that byelection in this round of votes "was no accident."

All parties have caps on how much they can spend promoting candidates during byelections. But the cap for a party increases if they're running candidates in multiple byelections and it's up to the party to decide how they want to distribute campaign funding amongst those ridings.
PM Carney to call 13 byelections in just 2 years

By calling two byelections in safe seats and one in a competitive Quebec riding, the Liberals had a spending advantage over the Bloc who only run candidates in that province. If Carney had included Saint-Hyacinthe-Bagot-Acton, it would have given the Bloc wiggle room to direct more campaign funding to Chicoutimi-Le Fjord.
"Clearly Carney has been very strategic in grouping the byelections in ways that will make sense for him," Turnbull said.
"I think that there will be machinations for sure to try to maintain a Liberal advantage in those [upcoming byelections], both financially and also in terms of just the overall ground game."
Grenier added that the Bloc might have concerns about how safe Saint-Hyacinthe-Bagot-Acton is after Monday.

"The Bloc is going to have to defend their seat … which, after the results in Chicoutimi, might make them sweat a bit," he said.
Of the six byelections coming, three will be in Quebec, two in Ontario (including in a safe Liberal Toronto seat, Scarborough North) and one in Saskatchewan.

In addition to the Bloc stronghold riding, Turnbull said she expects Carney will aim to use the timing of byelections to give his party some sort of advantage over the Conservatives in Brock's Ontario riding.
Once an MP officially resigns, the Speaker has to inform the chief electoral officer of the vacancy, at which point election rules state the prime minister has 11 to 180 days to call a byelection.
Because Savard-Tremblay stepped down in June, the last day that Carney can legally call the next byelection is Dec. 19.
